title: Malifaux Fourth Edition: Index of the Untold, Part I
content:
The first expansion book of Fourth Edition is here! Previously, Wyrd has followed a tried-and-tested formula for expansion books: a new Keyword for each faction, plus some new models for existing Keywords, and maybe a cycle of Versatiles. This time, though, we're doing something different. Index of the Untold does not have a single new model's rules in it. Or, from another perspective, it has billions of new models' rules in it.

That's because, for the first time since Second Edition, we've got an honest-to-Burning Man campaign book!

By now, seasoned wargamers are familiar with this formula. Whether you're talking about dedicated campaign-structured games like Necromunda and Trench Crusade, or well-developed campaign modes like Crusade and Path to Glory, the basic outline is well-trodden. Malifaux is in some ways uniquely ill-suited to this type of game mode, given that all of the Masters are specific named characters (and so are about half of their followers). So Wyrd has really swung for the fences here and created something incredibly cool that brings all the customization and narrative of a long-running campaign to the world of Malifaux.  I'm not normally a big narrative player and I am hugely excited to play a Malifaux campaign, so let's shuffle up our Fate decks and see what we've been dealt here!

Setting the Table

The book opens by describing the structure of a campaign, which will have seasoned narrative players nodding along.  A campaign is played in a series of games over several weeks. After each game, each player has an Aftermath step, whereupon you suffer lasting injuries, buy new equipment, add models to your roster (known as your Arsenal), and so on.  Every campaign has a meta-currency; Malifaux's is Scrip, which you use for buying sweet new Equipment and hiring on new fighters.

There are a few things that I'll mention here in passing but that you could probably already guess. You have a Campaign Rating, which is an overall measure of crew strength (as measured by injuries, equipment, and so on); the player with the lower Campaign Rating gets bonus Soulstones as a handicap in games. Game size is not fixed, but is capped at 6 stones higher than the total of the smallest roster involved in the game (six being, conveniently, the maximum number of starting Soulstones).  Wyrd reminds us that Malifaux really should not be played above 50 Soulstones, which is what it's balanced for, but hey, it's your campaign. Oh, and you can't ever gain abilities that affect hiring (for example, Wrath's Jam Session ability that lets him hire Crossroads models).  What you've picked is what you've got.

Wyrd also notes that this mode really only works if everyone is on the same page and is not rigorously balanced for matched play; basically, be cool. You are going to, hopefully, play these people again and again, so try not to twist the system until it snaps.  This is Rule 1 for pretty much any kind of miniature wargame campaign mode, so kudos to Wyrd for spelling it out.

"wait! i have one more book to return!" Credit: Wyrd Games

Gathering Your Forces

Starting at the beginning, you pick a Faction and two Keywords. At least one of your Keywords must be from the chosen Faction, but the other one can be from anywhere. The chosen Faction dictates your out-of-keyword and Versatile hiring pool, but that's it. Your two Keywords are combined, and models from either Keyword are treated as having both Keywords. This opens up some fairly insane combos, to begin with; I like the idea of hiring Dr. Meredith Stanley opposite pretty much anyone who repeatedly summons Peons (how about Jebediah?) but I bet you can think of some fun tricks on your own.  Remember Rule 1!

Once you've got your keywords, you have 25 Soulstones to hire your starting Arsenal. You can hire any model in your Keywords that has a Soulstone cost (so no hiring Witchling Thralls, for example). But you can't hire a Master or a Totem, and you don't get a Crew Card.

Why not?  You're building them!

That's the core of the campaign system: custom Masters and Crew Cards. Masters start off relatively weak and Totemless, but gain Advancements over the course of the campaign, including the ability to add on Totems and add abilities to their Crew Card.  By the end of the campaign you'll be playing custom Masters more broken than anything Reddit could come up with!

To begin with, you pick one of five Master archetypes, each of which sets your Master's Df, Wp, Sp, and Health, and decides its starting Actions and Abilities. Rather than fully custom Attacks and Abilities, your Master gets to borrow from other models in your Keyword pair (regardless of whether you've hired that exact model into your Arsenal). For example, a Heavy Hitter master gets to pick one Attack action from an ally model of cost 10 or less, plus one of its triggers, and one Tactical action from an ally of cost 5 or less. A Schemer, by contrast, gets just a single Attack action from an ally of cost 5 or less, but two different Tacticals from allies of cost 8 or less, and a front-of-card ability from an ally of cost 8 or less.  A Lucky Upstart even gets a piece of Equipment for free, which you can never lose!

You can pick your Master's base size (30-50mm) and Size (1-4), with no cost or penalty for going in either direction.  This is a bit odd to me, since both size and base size are very mechanically relevant in Malifaux, but I think this is an area where Wyrd expects you to be governed by Rule 1. You can choose traits like Construct or Living the same way (and the same comment applies). You also choose Bruiser or Strategist as an archetype, which affects only how your Master advances between games.  We will return to this later.

Next, you get a starting Crew Card, all of which are decidedly meh (by design - they'll get better!). There are 12 starting Crew Cards, each of which has exactly one ability. Sometimes this is an Action, sometimes it's a "when this model activates" or "when this model kills an enemy"-type ability, but in each case it costs a Soulstone: either to take the action or trigger the ability. These are designed to make any Keyword functional: one lets you attach Keyword-locked upgrades like Ophelia's guns, while another lets you create special Keyword Markers like Tide Markers and another lets you gain special Keyword Tokens like Voyage Tokens.  None of them is particularly efficient, but that's fine.  For now.

The Master archetypes mostly seem balanced to me, although it heavily depends on your Keyword. Picking Apex Amalgam encourages you to make a huge Heavy Hitter and borrow the Malisaurus's jaws or the Desolation Engine's, uh, horribly flailing thing, but Family crews might be fine picking a Generalist and borrowing Nino Ortega's sniper rifle.

Let's Get This Show on the Road

Once you've got your baby Master, your 25 stones of flunkies, and your starting Crew Card, that's it!  You're ready to play!

For the most part, setting up and playing campaign games is pretty easy; you just follow the standard rules for picking a Strategy, Deployment type, and Schemes. There's one modification to reflect the ongoing nature of the campaign: a Strategic Withdrawal. At the start of any turn, you can willingly bottle out - there's no check to see if it "succeeds" and it never happens unless you declare it, so it's a fully voluntary choice.  If you do so on turns 1 or 2, you skip your entire postgame Aftermath step except rolling for injuries.  Otherwise it's just a normal loss; your opponent can spend the rest of the game (probably) maxing out their score, and if you somehow still win the game even though you fled, your score is automatically set to one lower than your opponent.  No rewards for cowardice!

Once the game is done, either normally or through Strategic Withdrawal, you move into the postgame step.  And that's where the magic happens.

yessss... that's right... give me all your scrip... Credit: Wyrd Games

Last Laugh in the Aftermath

The "Aftermath" is where the bulk of the campaign rules are located, and it fittingly takes up the majority of the campaign section of the book.  (There is another section of the book, though, as we will see!).

An Aftermath step is broken into six phases, and we'll tackle them one at a time.  They are:

  • Draw Aftermath Hand
  • Payday
  • Barter
  • Advance Leader
  • Back-Alley Doctor
  • Determine Injuries

A note as we proceed: The term for "permanently removed from your roster" is Annihilated, which can happen to Injuries, Equipment, and even models, most notably when they acquire their third Injury. The first time your Master is annihilated, they avoid fate and cross off their third injury (if they have one); the second time, they're done, and so is their crew.  You are invited to start fresh.

Draw Aftermath Hand

Simple and straightforward.  This is Malifaux - we're not sending you into the wilds of Random Number Generation without a few cheats in your pocket.  You shuffle up your deck and deal yourself a hand of variable size: one card for completing a game without Withdrawing, and then one card for each Scheme you completed, to a maximum of 3.  Just scoring one point from a Scheme counts as completing it, but you can't get four cards this way by going 1-1-2-2, so your endgame hand caps at 4.  These cards can be cheated for any postgame flip: barter, advancement, back-alley doctor or injury flips.  You can't empower, mind you: these flips are never at a +twist.

You also have to do all postgame flips one at a time, fully resolving each before you move on to the next.  There's an element of tension there: you may want to save your cards if your flip isn't that bad, but if it turns out your later flips are better, you can't go back.  You have to make decisions with the information you have.

Once you draw your hand, you do not shuffle again.  What you've got is what you've got, and it's got to last you to the end.

Payday

Another simple one.  You earn one one Scrip postgame for every 3 points you earned, rounding up (so 4 points = 2 Scrip).  You get one more if you won, and one more, win or lose, if you had the lower Campaign Rating.  Maxing out your score and winning with a lower Campaign Rating, then, is worth 6 Scrip.

Scrip persists week to week, so don't feel compelled to spend it all at once!  One final note: adding new models to your Arsenal is done at the start of a week, before you play your first game, not as part of the Aftermath. Hiring a model into the Arsenal simply requires you to spend its Soulstone cost in Scrip, plus 1 if it's an out-of-keyword, non-Versatile model from your declared Faction.  You must hire at least one new model each week (barring your first week - the step is skipped for that week), but the first model you hire each week gets a steep 5-Scrip discount.

Barter

Now we're talking.  For everyone but your Master, this is where advances come from. (Your Master can barter, too, but they also get a special advance table). Barter is where you spend hard-earned Scrip on Equipment.

Bartering opens with a Barter flip - a single card off the deck, which tells you what's in stock this week.  The Equipment table is massive, and consists of four "always available" entries plus six entries per card value, 1-13.  These are further separated by suit into "ram or mask" and "tome or crow," so if you flip, say, the Four of Tomes, you can buy the Fool's Gold, Useless Generator and Gatling Gun. And remember you can cheat this!

That means you typically have seven options available to you each time you flip, and you can buy as many as you have Scrip for.  None of the items are unique, with one qualified exception.

Equipment is a dizzying array of buffs, impossible to summarize.  Broadly, you can separate it into three categories: items that give you a new action, items that give you a new passive ability, and consumables.  Consumables can be Annihilated to have a one-time effect; for example, the always-available Lucky Gremlin's Foot lets you no-sell a single Injury for the low cost of one Scrip.

Many of the actions and abilities are familiar - I can see Juggernaut (from the Guardian's Shield), Don't Turn Your Back (from the Trickster's Mask), and Lure (from the False Face).  But the majority of them are brand new, and some are extremely cool.  Special shout-outs go to the Quick-Draw Holster, which lets you pitch a card to treat any action as a Signature; the Dead Man's Switch (which gives you a 3" pulse, 3 irreducible damage Demise); and the Strange Portal, which can be Annihilated when a model activates to let you flip a card (which cannot be cheated) and resolve an effect based on the result.  Flip a crow and your model "dies" (without flipping for a postgame injury), only to appear, in exactly the state he or she is in now, on turn 1 of the next game you play.  Flip a joker? Your opponent summons an exact doppelganger of your model (presumably with a natty goatee), and you get 1 VP if you take out the imposter during the game.

Rosie with Arcane Sense and Quick Draw Holster enables some extremely funny plays. Credit: Wyrd Games

If you flip the Black Joker, you simply don't get anything (aside from the Always Available stuff).  But flipping the Red Joker lets you flip on the special Those Who Thirst table, a table of rare and powerful relic weapons. Note that only flipping the Red gives you access to this table; cheating it merely gives you a 13 of the suit of your choice.,  You can only have one of Those Who Thirst, so you flip the red again later in the campaign you "ignore this result"; personally I would just treat a second flip on the table as a cheated Red (a 13 of the player's choice), but I'm not your dad and I can't tell you how to live your life.

Those Who Thirst are pretty cool, though.  The Book of the Dead is a long-range, damage 3 magical attack that summons a Mindless Zombie onto the target, plus one for each raise you get. The Medusa, meanwhile, does just one point of damage but Slows, Stuns and Entrances the target.  All of these relic weapons come with a crow trigger, Laid to Rest, that causes anyone taken out by them to make two injury flips and apply both results - this is brutal, but it's sufficiently rare that I don't mind seeing it.  There's even a special result on the Those Who Thirst table for flipping "either joker," by which I guess Wyrd means the Black Joker, since you have to have flipped the Red to even be here.  Anyways, the Red-into-Black result is Omen's Mark, an equipment you must attach to someone every game and which causes its bearer to take an additional damage from all sources.  The kicker is that when the model is killed, the model that killed it takes up the Omen's Mark, and your crew loses it - and this is the only way to get rid of it, as it cannot be discarded or annihilated.

Once purchased, Equipment sits in your Arsenal.  At the start of any game, a piece of Equipment can be attached to any of your models, and it's never locked to that model - as long as you have the thing, you can pass it around between games as much as you want. Equipment can be discarded in various ways, but unless it's Annihilated, it always returns to your Arsenal to be used again.

I love the Barter table.  It's colossal and a ton of love and thought has clearly gone into making these entries exciting even for veteran players.  I will say that I do not love that cheating the Red does not give you access to the relic table; this is a persistent theme through the postgame steps, and I understand the purpose is to make the "Red Joker table" results rarer and more exciting, but in practice it means that drawing the Red in your postgame hand kind of sucks, as it locks you out of getting these cool results.  At minimum, I'd probably want to play with a house rule that flipping or cheating the Red Joker results in it being immediately shuffled back into the deck, if only so the "Red into Joker" results will happen more than once a century.

Advance Leader

Once you have done all your shopping, it's time for your Master to advance!  Remember when you picked Bruiser or Strategist?  Now is the time for it to pay off - after each game you get experience points, as follows:

  • One for showing up, which is half the battle;
  • One if you are a Bruiser and killed one or more non-Peon models during a game;
  • One if you are a Strategist and resolved at least one Interact within 6" of the enemy Deployment Zone; and
  • One if you lost the game.  Failure is the best teacher!

That means the maximum you can get is 3 points after a game, although there is Equipment that grants experience points under certain conditions.

you're gonna need all the experience points you can get, buddy. Credit: Wyrd Games

There's a Master advancement track, which consists of 39 sequential boxes; 24 are blank, and 15 have a number from 1-4 in them.  When you get experience points, you just start markin' boxes, and when you mark a box with a number in it, congrats!  It's advancing time!

When you get an advance, you simply flip on the appropriate table.  There are four tables, although you have some flexibility here: you can flip on a lower table than the number in the box you just checked.  I will note that the first three boxes on the track are marked 1, 1, 2, so it doesn't take long for Masters to start differentiating themselves, although advances get more sparse with time.

The advance tables come in four categories, although they have some elements in common.  They don't have Suits like the Barter table; instead, whatever number you flip, you can pick any entry of that number or lower.  Given that the tables have 2-5 entries per number, that can give you a pretty staggering range of choices.  There are two tables in each tier 1-3; Tier 4 is special, and we'll get to that one. When you flip, you can pick either table in a given tier to flip in.

Tier 1

Tier 1 consists of Attack and Tactical action modifications, which add triggers to your existing actions, increase your Skl, or make an action Signature. You can apply these triggers to an action you gained from Equipment, although doing so means your Master must be the one to use that equipment in every game from now on (no sharing!) and if you lose the equipment for whatever reason, the advance goes with it.  In addition, when adding a trigger to action with 2 or more triggers already, you must pay 2 scrip for the privilege.

The new Action triggers are mostly pre-existing, although there are some fun new ones, like Wild Toss (for one Soulstone, place the target within 5" and deal a point of damage to it). The Joker triggers are neat as well: for the Attack actions, one is just Good for a Laugh, but for a Soulstone, but the other one can be declared when killing the enemy Leader and gives your Master +1 experience points after the game.  Good show!  There are also Joker Tactical action triggers, one of which lets you ditch your Scheme and pick a new one without telling your opponent what you ditched.

Tier 2

This Tier of advances gives you new abilities, either Actions or front-of-card passives.  The Actions are, as before, not new, but they're really good ones: I see Ulix's Hellfire Shot, Zipp's Zipp Zapper, and old favorites like Steamroller, Leap and Secret Passage.

The Abilities, meanwhile, are mostly workhorses like Butterfly Jump, Serene Countenance, Flight, and Trample, but there are some spicy ones here: I particularly like Entourage and Fortify the Spirit.  The "always available" abilities are new too: they all cost a Soulstone to use, but include a free 4" teleport at start of activation and a Soulstone-powered defensive ability that reduces damage by 2 to a minimum of 0.

Flipping a Joker here lets you pick any action/ability from a model in either of your Keywords with a cost of up to 10, just like at the start of the campaign, which is both wild and hilarious.

Tier 3

This tier is a bit different from the others. For one thing, you don't get to pick any result equal to or below your flip: what you flip is what you get. For another, the second table doesn't even let you flip at all.

The first table is Totem Advancements. The name is slightly misleading: the advancement is getting a Totem at all.  There are, of course, 15 options, none of which map directly onto any existing Totem; each one comes with a set of stats (Df, Wp, Sp, Health), and some abilities, Attack actions and/or Tactical actions. Once you earn the Totem you get it fully formed, and there's no point flipping on the table again unless your Totem got Annihilated or you really don't like the one you got.  You pick your Totem's base size, Sz, and traits (undead, living, etc.), up to two traits, at time of hiring. From then on, when your Master would earn an Advance, you may choose to Advance your totem instead.

I have to say I like some of these a lot. I am a special fan of the Willing Vessel, a fat sack of HP with the Emissaries' Tempting Fate ability, plus an Attack and Tactical Action that both heal the Vessel.  There is a special place in my heart, though, for the Sniveling Coward, the Black Joker totem; he sucks at everything, but if he damages an enemy model and then survives to the end of the game, you can permanently replace him with any non-Joker totem, keeping any Advances he's earned.

The Red Joker totem is a bit disappointing: he just gains an Action on the printed stat card of a Master that shares a keyword with yours (i.e. a real Master, from Malifaux), but without any triggers, and with no other abilities, and also you can't copy actions that list a model by name or transform the user. The idea of copying the .950 Nitro Express is very funny, but realistically, the best use for this is to just copy a summoning ability.

sadly, this one doesn't work because her summon names Seishin. Credit: Wyrd Games

The second table is Summoning Advancements.  You can only ever pick this once, and you don't flip - you just choose an option from a table.  These advancements give you the ability to summon a model, and since most keywords don't have models with Summon TNs, the abilities on this table work a little differently than the summons you're used to.  There are 7, each of which gives you the ability to summon a model of your Keyword pair - typically of cost 5 or less, but one ability is locked to cost 3 or less and another only summons peons.  There are a variety of different conditions here: remove an enemy marker, remove a friendly marker near an enemy, remove a friendly token from an enemy model, etc.

I understand the strict limits on Summons: it really breaks the game to have good repeatable summons, since you don't care if they die but your opponent really does care if they lose models.  Summoning models whose entire purpose is to fight and die can inflict serious damage on your opponent's crew even if you lose the game. There are enough safety valves on the Summon Advancements that they're probably fine, but it does just highlight how the Mini-Master totem can break the mode: if you're in a Keyword pair that includes at least one high-powered summoner (DUA, say, or Witch Hunter), you can just focus on breaking your opponents' kneecaps with summons and catching up later in the campaign season.

Tier 4

Tier 4 is Crew Card upgrades, and there's no table here at all.  Instead, when you choose this result, you simply pick ONE effect printed on any crew card associated with your Keywords (typically 4 crew cards total - one for each title of each Master - although some weirdos like Kastore have more), and add it to your crew card.  There are some rules:

  • No power bars and no rules that swap the crew card for another one.
  • One "effect" is one ability, action, or trigger.  That's it.  And you can only pick a trigger if that trigger is listed individually on the card (the example in the book is Crack Skulls on the Excessive Violence crew card).
  • Actions come with their associated triggers.

You can also choose one of the starting campaign crew card rules to add to your crew card, though I think you will rarely want to do this.

I have to say this is a little disappointing.  I agree that it was important to unlock base-game crew card rules, since so many of them are integral to how their Keywords function, but it would have been really nice to see a little table of custom crew card effects. Some crew cards also have two-part rules where each individual part does nothing - think Audit Reality/Contaminated Theories from Footnotes of Madness, or Astronomical Observations/The Stars Shift from Study the Stars.

Back-Alley Doctor

After you've spent those precious experience points, it's time to visit the ol' sawbones!  Note that this comes before the Determine Injuries step, so you'll have to play at least one game with your boo-boo before you can have the nice man kiss it away.

Actually, a kiss might have better medicinal value than what ol' doc here is working with. You spend 1 scrip to try to heal an injury and then flip a card. Naturally, the Black Joker results in you getting another injury for your pains (which will be agonizing), but a 1-8 does nothing, and a 9 just swaps your injury for another, potentially worse one. On a 10 or 11 you heal your injury but end up Undead ("That still counts as healed") or a Construct ("Took some spare parts, but we got there"), while a 12 or 13 is an unqualified success.  Flipping (not cheating) the Red Joker gets you a flip on the Lucky Miss table, which we'll see in a moment when we get to the Injuries section (but it's your stock "actually, this injury was a good thing, and this isn't blood in my mouth but victory wine" table).

Not too much to say here; I like that getting rid of injuries isn't easy, but in practice you'll just save your high cards and cheat the result you need here.  If a model is really messed up, though, you might as well take a swing at healing them.  What have you got to lose (besides your scrip)?

Injuries

Ahhh, yes.  Here we go.  Everyone's favorite part of campaign play: now you figure out what happened when your favorite character was shot, stabbed, set on fire, and pushed off the roof.

Peons can't be injured, but everyone else who died during a game has to flip. This table follows the same "masks/rams, crows/tomes" setup as the Equipment table, but has just one result per card.  If you double up, you just skip getting an injury, so... lucky you!  Can't lose your right foot twice.

As noted, once you get three injuries, you're toast!

no, that's - nevermind. Credit: Wyrd Games

In a reversal of fortune, 1s and 2s here are good - you don't get injured - whereas 13s mean instant death.  Everything else is varying degrees of bad.  Models with a Dulled Edge suffer -1 Df, while Senseless models must discard a card every time they activate or gain Slow, and models with Brittle Bones give everyone (mostly enemies, but sometimes friendlies!) a +twist on all attack flips against them.

There are a few very cool injuries, I have to say. Blood Debt lets you spend a Soulstone while in the opposing deployment zone to Annihilate the injury permanently - but if you don't do that during your game, your opponent can Annihilate it at the end to give themselves an extra VP!  The Red Joker lets you flip on the Lucky Miss table, of which more in a second, while the Black makes you a Traitor - the model is Annihilated from your roster (unless it's a master or totem, who can't turn stag), and your opponent adds it to their Arsenal with all of its injuries and equipment intact!

The Lucky Miss table is, as you might expect, all buffs. They're really good ones, too: Secret Directive gives you a bonus VP if that model ends the game within 6" of the enemy deployment zone, while The Hunter lets you infuse a Soulstone every time you kill an enemy. Flipping the black on this table gives you a Doppelganger: you get a copy of whatever model it was added to your Arsenal, with all injuries and equipment intact.  Yes, this can copy your Master.  Yes, then you get two Masters.  Yes, the second copy is free.

It's fine.  This is gonna come up once in every 50 campaigns and it's going to be hilarious when it does.

On the Warpath

That's it!  That's all of the campaign rules!  Go forth and conquer!

Wait, you want to know who wins?  Everyone wins because you had fun with your friends!

Ok, fine.  There are Competitive Campaign rules, and a bunch of other optional twists and modifiers.  There's also an entirely new way to play Malifaux in this book.  But that'll have to wait until Part II of this review, which is already almost 5000 words long.  Until next time, Mali-folks!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? title: This epic new Lord of the Rings board game is a dynamic roll-and-write where you play both sides of the battle
content:
Certain themes are dime-a-dozen in board games. Trains. Space. Dune (which I guess also counts as Space). The Lord of the Rings also has a place on that list, especially in recent years. It feels like Asmodee and its subsidiaries have pumped out a new journey through Middle-earth every month of the 2020s.

And guess what? It's not done yet. This year's Gen Con showed off multiple upcoming Lord of the Rings board games, each finding different ways to chuck a ring into a volcano. For me, the most unique by far was The Lord of the Rings: Circle of Conflict.

Releasing in November 2026, this is Office Dog's next Middle-earth adventure. After it published the absolute slammer that is The Lord of the Rings Trick-Taking Game, my hopes were high. Now I've demoed Circle of Conflict myself, my hopes are even higher.

This might be the first Lord of the Rings board game where you play as both the Free Peoples and the Shadow. Your Free Peoples battle the Shadow of the opponent on your left, while your Shadow tackles the Free Peoples of the player on your right. This is, after all, a Circle of Conflict.

This mishmash of priorities gives you four possible ways to win. Your Free Peoples want to get the Ring to Mordor by moving the Fellowship across its map. Meanwhile, the Shadow can win by corrupting the Fellowship completely before this happens. Either side can also win by besting their enemy in two battles.

Already, there are a lot of crunchy moving pieces to chew on. Your web of choices gets even broader when you look at how these wins are achieved.

Circle of Conflict is a roll-and-write. This is a genre I usually associate with simple, solitary, soothing gameplay. Circle of Conflict is none of these things. Instead, it's tense and tactical, with huge diversity in decisions.

Each round begins with the 'roll' part of roll-and-write. Two white dice are rolled, and all players must pick one to assign to their Free Peoples and one for their Shadow. The icons on the dice decide what symbols you can mark on the respective halves of your board.

Before you get drawing, though, a little Smeagol meeple (a Smeaple?) might move around a track. Rolling rings sets him off, and when he passes certain thresholds, players get to add resources to one of their teams. These are 'Hunt' or 'Resolve'.

After that tricksy little segment, players mark their newly-acquired resource icons and decide what public and secret actions they'll take. The main secret action you'll take is for your Free Peoples, and it's Move the Fellowship. Spend Resolve by erasing it from your board, and you can mark a new location on your board's leftmost map of Middle-Earth. There are several routes you can take to get the Ring to Mordor, but choose carefully - because the hunt is on.

Hunting the Fellowship is a public action that's unique to the Shadow. You spend Hunt to activate it, and the number of Hunt erased must equal the value of a location on your map. This is the location that you'll declare as your target - the one you think your opponent's Fellowship is currently hiding at.

Guess incorrectly, and your opponent must tell you how many spaces away (by the shortest route) their Fellowship is. Guess right, and you can spend additional Hunt to erase that much Resolve from your opponent's board. If their Resolve is already at zero, you mark two spaces on your Corruption track.

Here lies the push-and-pull part of Circle of Conflict. You're watching your opponents like a hawk, trying to zone in on their Fellowship while concealing your own. Racing to Mount Doom (to take the 'Destroy the Ring' action and win) is no good if someone guesses that you took the shortest, most obvious path. But maybe a double-bluff will win you the day? Or maybe Corruption is the more efficient route.

That's just half of the game's strategy. The rest lies in your remaining public actions, which are shared by both sides.

Firstly, you can Activate a Nation when you've filled in enough squares on its track. This unlocks their die, which is rolled in future rounds, with its resources available only to those who activated said nation. Advance that same track even further, and you can Motivate a Nation to gain double value from the icons on its die.

Activating and motivating nations also gives you immediate resources to spend, which can be used to advance character tracks or muster certain troops. Characters with complete tracks can lend a hand in battles through actions (or reactions), but they have uses elsewhere too. Gandalf, for example, makes your Fellowship harder to detect and corrupt.

As for Mustering, this is a public action you'll want to do plenty of. Once a troop's track is filled, you can take the Muster action to add to your army strength. Army strength is how you win one of those two crucial battles.

To battle, you'll take the March action, declaring your intended battlefield. This must be done three times, with an actual fight taking place once the third March track space is marked. Your battle is worth a base one victory point, unless you previously took the Commitment action to raise its value to two or three VP.

The player that takes the March action is the attacker, and the Defender gets a +3 bonus to their army strength straight away. That strength is mainly determined by your mustered forces, plus any character actions you wish to take during battle.

Fight two battles, and the game's winner is whoever has the most victory points. Note that you also get end-game points for every 10 army strength you have in a battle space, even if it is never resolved.

With only two shots at victory, battles are a cautious, calculated thing. Your decisions are made even more impactful by all those tracks you're marking on your player board. While some resources can be spent and regained at will, your most powerful actions are single-use. Knowing when to deploy them to clinch the win is crucial - and challenging.

Circle of Conflict is one of those games I'll need repeat plays to fully master. For now, all I'll say is this: I'm yet to feel fatigued by Lord of the Rings board games. This timeless story keeps managing to be interesting on the tabletop.

title: Detachment Focus: Frenzied Host
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we take a deep dive into an army’s Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this Detachment Focus we’re looking at the Frenzied Host Detachment for the Emperor's Children.

The Emperor's Children were in a weird place coming into 11th edition, heavily dependent on Defilers for competitive play and then suddenly saddled with the reality that the army's best Detachment - Coterie of the Conceited - was labeled a 3 DP Detachment and given Priority Assets as a disposition - not ideal for an elite army with few action units. Fortunately the Frenzied Host Detachment has been a major boon for the army, helping other Detachments punch up by turning the army into a kind of "World Eaters lite" with combat bonuses whenever you Advance or Fall Back.

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Disruption

The Emperor's Children tend to rely on a melee-heavy approach to combat, owing partly to a lack of good ranged options. Unfortunately, their melee options, particularly those on Infractors - the army's workhorse - tend to be a bit lackluster, with just a large number of S4, AP-1 attacks and a reliance on Lords Exultant and [LETHAL HITS] to punch up into heavier targets. Frenzied Host helps with that substantially, giving your battleline units +1S when a unit makes an Advance or Fall Back move. Your Battleline units here are Tormentors and Infractors, both of which commonly show up in Emperor's Children lists.

This Detachment is all about your Battleline units and has the unique HOST tag, meaning it can’t be taken with other HOST Detachments. Specifically, that means you can't double up with this and Mercurial Host.

Detachment Rule: Frantic Focus

When a friendly Emperor’s Children Battleline unit is selected to make an Advance or Fall Back move, that unit’s attacks have +1 S until the end of the turn.

This is a very solid ability. One of the key challenges that you’ll face with your Infractors is that they’re only throwing out S4 AP-1 attacks, and while you have a good volume of those, you’re going to lose a lot of them to failed wound rolls against T4 and T5 targets. You normally get around this by adding a Lord Exultant, but that only goes so far, and is better for punching up into high-Toughness targets. This lets you more effectively convert attacks into kills and punch up into T8 and T9 targets. It’s particularly good on the Lord Exultant, where going to S8 with [LANCE] helps you hit key breakpoints and wound units with T5-7 on a 2+.

This rule notably also doesn’t specify melee attacks, so your Tormentors can benefit as well, buffing their plasma gun and meltagun - having a S10 meltagun is a pretty solid deal. Just be sure to keep tabs on when and where you're falling back and charging so you don't run afoul of the thrill seekers restrictions on which units you can charge or shoot.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

  • Euphoric Crown. Lord Exultant only. The model’s melee attacks have +1 S. Now we’re getting indulgent, but in a good way. The idea here is that your Lord Exultant can go to either S9 on his spear (with LANCE) or S10 on his power fist whenever you advance or fall back and charge. S9 on the Spear is likely the better deal of the two, as you’ll be charging often with him while he’s alive. Being S9 instead of S8 gets you past some interesting break points like Rhinos and Bloat-Drones, but there aren’t that many T9/10 threats.
  • Howling Plate. Lord Exultant only. The unit’s ranged attacks have +1 AP. This is potentially pretty solid, giving you AP-1 on things like bolter shots and AP-4 on overcharged plasma. Getting good value out of this mostly means putting a Lord Exultant on a 10-model unit of Tormentors, though - and that’s just not really what you want to be doing with an Emperor’s Children army.

Stratagems

  • Possessive Mania (1 CP). Used in your opponent’s Shooting phase or the Fight phase when an opponent targets one of your BATTLELINE units in range of an objective. Attacks targeting your unit have -1 AP until the end of that attack sequence. This is a very situational Armour of Contempt, and while that’s a very solid ability (especially in melee), it’s also pretty limited. It definitely has more play in 11th, where you no longer get a bonus to your save from cover.
  • Agonised Cacophony (1 CP). Used at the start of your Shooting phase to pick an enemy unit that is within 12” of one of your BATTLELINE units and visible to it. That unit gets +6” Detection Range. Shooting in EC is pretty limited, and the units you have who can shoot tend to be pretty fast and they can all Advance and Shoot. Which is all to say that most of the time you won’t need this.
  • Absolute Sensory Overload (1 CP). Used in your Shooting phase, when a BATTLELINE unit shoots. That unit’s ranged attacks won’t prevent it from being hidden. This is cute, and can be helpful if you need to shoot your way out of some trouble near your home objective, but it’s pretty situational.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

The Enhancements here are solid buffs for your Lord Exultants and the Stratagems are only OK. What this amounts to is that you're here for the Detachment ability, which is very good on its own. It gives you much more consistent output into marine-shaped targets and helps you punch up more effectively into bigger threats with units which otherwise struggle to contribute. Every Emperor's Children army takes Infractors, and having a Detachment to make them shine helps the army across the board. It's worth noting that the Detachment rule here won't work on Daemonettes despite those being BATTLELINE; they lack the EMPEROR'S CHILDREN keyword.

Because of the simple nature of this buff and the passive benefit, you can pair this Detachment with any of the other 2 DP options, giving you immediate support, even if the Disposition you get - Disruption - isn't worth taking. The key is to always be falling back or advancing with key units, but you were already doing that anyways.

Strengths

  • Really strong Detachment ability that makes common units much more effective
  • Good Lord Exultant buffs

Weaknesses

  • Mediocre Stratagems

A Sample List

Here's a great example of a Frenzied Host list, combining the detachment with Carnival of Excess in a Recon build. It's a common top list for Emperor's Children right now, using Daemonettes to score recon and act as cheap, dangerous wide threats while Exultant-led Infractors can handle anything in the middle of the table. Conan Jennings took this list to a 5-0, 1st place finish at the Gem City GT in early August.

Final Thoughts

If you're running Emperor's Children, Frenzied Host are going to be a common competitive pick. The Detachment ability is strong, easy to remember and use, and goes on units you were already taking anyways. title: GW shocks Warhammer 40k fans with new Nob pics
content:
On Monday, Games Workshop revealed a brand new kit for the Ork Nobz. Nobz are the bigger and meaner veteran troops of the belligerent greenskin race; their name is both an abbreviation of the word 'Noble' and a puerile joke that a Warhammer 40k writer came up with in the late 1980s, and headline writers have been grateful for ever since. The updated Nobz are set to release some time after the Orks get their new 11th edition codex, and will bring a few new toys into the new edition.

According to GW's post on the Warhammer community website announcing the kit, the new Nobz can "be beefed up with a bunch of specialist gear". We don't know all of the implements of destruction that these big lunks will get to play with, but model pictures reveal that they will at least include a whopping great Big Skorcha, and some very large guns that aren't just the current Kombi-Shoota option.

While it seems the Nobz will gain some ranged weapons, they're going to lose some melee options. Specifically, the rules for their melee weapons will be streamlined so that various "powered blades, klaws, and bludgeons" will be rolled into a single profile for "Kustom Krumpas". It's still possible that certain melee weapons will get singled out with unique profiles; that massive Big Choppa really looks like it deserves to have the Cleave ability.

GW also shared some new angles on the previously revealed new Ork Warbiker kit. They look sick! And there's at least one minor change to their statline: the biker Nob can now add a Rokkit launcher to their mount for a little bit of tank-punching power.

1/3

The updated Warbikers will release before the Nobz and alongside the new Orks' Codex. That doesn't give us a firm date, but it will be soon, with Orks the first Warhammer 40k faction to receive a new Codex this edition.

If you want to share pics of your Nobz, they'll be welcome in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: The $60 mythic Badgermole MTG card is finally banned
content:
Wizards of the Coast has revealed the August 10 MTG banlist update for Magic: The Gathering, and this one makes much-needed changes to multiple formats. For starters, that Fantasticar oversight which allowed players to dish out 16 damage on turn one has been cleaned up, with the card getting axed in Vintage and Legacy.

But perhaps more importantly, and for most fans far more relevantly: Badgermole Cub and Stormchaser's Talent are both receiving bans in Standard.

Badgermole Cub is single-handedly responsible for green's return to prominence. Its value was unrivaled, creating a body and a ridiculous amount of ramp for a mere two drop, and allowing green decks to reach their big stompy cards with frightening speed..

While I think more fans will be celebrating the little green burrower's demise (the sadists!) Stormchaser's Talent has been at least as big a problem. In fact, this ban is probably overdue by a year or more, as the Talent has helped blue-red decks be a completely dominant force for more than a year. Over the months, the meta shifted, but Izzet has always been at or near the top.

Wizards says it chose not to ban these cards because,"the gap between these two strategies and the rest of the format was discernable but not insurmountable, and many decks could find success each weekend".

In essence, the two cards here suffered from a similar design problem. They are both very cheap cards that create multiple pieces of value, making it hard to efficiently answer them. At the same time they also have effects that threaten to snowball out of control and run away with the game.

Alongside this pair of ne'er-do-wells is a rather unexpected ban. Gran-Gran, another card from the Avatar: The Last Airbender set, is no more! This card was a key part of the Lessons deck's engine, both adding cards to the graveyard and giving your spells a discount. Poor Gran-Gran. Look at her there waving us goodbye.

Apparently WotC took out both Stormchaser's Talent and Gran-Gran to deprive Jeskai Lessons and Izzet Prowess of one card each, and hopefully stop blue-red from swarming the format now Badgermole Cub is gone. It'll be interesting to see if that attempt was successful!

title: Preview: 13 Omens is pure TTRPG terror from the studio that brought you Pathfinder
content:
Horror is one of the most enduring genres in tabletop RPGs. Every system dips its toe into something spooky at least once, it seems. This is a little surprising, though, as real horror in an RPG is hailed as nigh-impossible to achieve. A reliance on the intangible - and the party's constant desire to be goofy little guys - make true terror difficult to manifest.

That being said, 13 Omens is a horror slam-dunk. Its incredibly simple rules (surprising, I know, from the designers of Pathfinder) are tailor-made for tense one-shots. The system only needs a few standout mechanics to make you feel nervous. And I was very nervous in my demo game at Gen Con.

The omens

13 Omens follows in the footsteps of two of my favorite tabletop RPGs: Ten Candles and Dread. Both are designed for horror one-shots, and both employ props to make the terror more tangible. Dread swaps dice rolls for a Jenga tower, which kills a character off if they cause it to topple. Ten Candles, meanwhile, snuffs out candles with every failed roll, and everyone dies when the last goes out.

13 Omen's schtick is dice in a bag. Every time a roll is called, the player pulls two D6s from a dark bag. The result of these is compared with a Target Number consisting of your proficiency in the relevant stat and difficulty modifiers decided by the Host.

"The host, the person who runs the game, doesn't roll dice at all", Joe Pasini, lead designer of 13 Omens, tells me. It's very much a player-led system, but the Host has a unique way to influence play. "They add dangerous dice to the bag to make it scarier."

These dice are your titular 13 Omens. A game begins with just one of these different-colored d6s in the bag, but the Host gradually adds them during play. They tend to appear when characters interact with the evil force plaguing them - or attempt an action that's particularly risky.

"The physical act of reaching into a dark bag and hoping you don't pull something bad is really compelling", Pasini tells me. He doesn't really need to tell me, though, as the demo says it all for him. The tension is palpable when a bag pull is called for. You could slash it with a blade.

It's not quite as tangible a fear as in Ten Candles or Dread, though. Those games' props have more capacity for metaphor than a pool of D6s. A sputtering candle or a teetering tower is always going to be more evocative than pips on a die. Still, 13 Omens gets a lot of mileage out of these relatively abstract objects.

Plus, dice have perks of their own. They're an accessible entry point to roleplay, and they offer more mechanical flexibility. Ready for a shock twist before act two? 13 Omens has found even more interesting ways to mess with our math cubes.

The victims

Omen dice also represent how badly a character is wounded by their trials. Each begins life totally unscathed (lucky them), but once the horror shows begin, the pain comes thick and fast. "This is three or four hours of ratcheting tension", Pasini says, "and it's all about attrition". "You're losing power as you go, you're getting more scared, and worse things are happening."

There are two currencies to track your suffering. The first is Strain, a mark that affects your Aspects (stats) by adding a Flaw to their future rolls. When rolling with a Flaw, you draw a third die from the bag, roll all three, then take the lowest two as your final result.

There is an opposite positive effect in the form of Edge, which lets you take the highest two rolls. Either way, however, you're drawing more dice from the bag - which makes getting an Omen die more likely.

This is utterly awful thanks to our second currency: Wounds. When you roll an Omen dice and your result is lower than the current 'Act' of the game (one, two, or three), you take a Wound. That Omen die leaves the current pool (yay!) and is placed on your character sheet (less yay!).

Gain four Wounds, and you're dead meat. Or you're traumatized beyond repair. Or something worse. Whatever torment your Host dreams up, it means you're out of the game.

As the Wounds and Strain rack up, every move you make could mean disaster. It keeps you on the edge of your seat, and you weigh up every choice.

I felt painfully human during my demo demo. I took fewer Wounds than everybody else, so was expected to lead the charge into danger - but a few bad rolls could change everything. What if I don't make that jump across the chasm? What if going first - or last - in the marching order puts me in the firing line of whatever lurks in the dark?

Omen dice are nerve-wracking, in the bag or on your character sheet. "When everybody is near death, you're on a knife's edge", Pasini adds. "If anyone dies, all their bad dice go back in the bag - and are more likely to be drawn." "This really cascades in a fun way in later acts."

The house of horrors

Let's talk about those 'acts'. Every game of 13 Omens follows a three-act structure, like an actual scary movie. Act two triggers when the fifth Omen die enters the bag, and act three begins after the ninth is added. By the time the final die is added, the story is wrapping up, with characters' fates all but sealed.

"The three-act structure really lends itself to, as I call it, 'getting the giggles out'", Pasini tells me. "I've played a lot of horror games where you're with friends and goofing around, and sometimes that means horror games don't feel scary enough." "In act one, you have the freedom to goof around and get to know the characters", he explains. "It's very low stakes, and then it naturally gets scarier - people get really invested in ways I haven't seen in other games."

Speaking from experience, act one gives you time to get your bearings. Your personality is summed up by a handful of stats (Courage, Evade, Fight, Luck, Perception, plus a few story-specific aspects), two unique perks, and the gear in your bag. The details are up to you to hash out through play, and act one is the perfect breeding ground for personal quirks.

Act two, though, is where you find out who you really are. The monster of the week rears its ugly head for the first time, and you see who panic turns you into. Me? I was eager but inexperienced, flip-flopping between total cowardice and rushing hastily into danger to prove myself (and protect my friends).

13 Omens' pacing is one of its major strengths, giving you space to live out these complex character arcs before giving you a gruesome on-screen death. A few extra rules act as additional support beams.

For example, if you happen to die uncharacteristically early, "the Host can decide not to kill you yet - and wait for a more dramatic moment to snuff out your life." "There's also rules that let you participate even when you're dead", Pasini explains. "You can use a flashback to say 'remember when I put this in your bag earlier?' and help the living characters out of a tough spot."

Roll credits

One taste is never truly enough to assess a tabletop RPG. I'll need more testing time to determine if the balance of each act is as stable as Paizo says. Plus, as eager as I am to play 13 Omens again, I want to see if I feel the same after five games, or 10. One-shot systems must struggle harder for replayability than your average Pathfinder or D&D.

Right now, all I can give you is a first impression - but what a spectacular one. Paizo set out to create a system with a narrow scope and a simple execution. Somehow, that's manifested as an emotional, effective RPG that scratches all my horror itches. Can't wait for my schlock story to get a sequel.

title: Warhammer 40k spinoff Necromunda gets more glorious Goliath muscle daddies
content:
Last week I reported on the new Escher matriarch miniatures for Warhammer 40k spinoff Necromunda, which I described as "queer-coded warrior women". This was met with some pushback from social media commentators, arguing that - because the Escher were based on the notoriously heterosexual punk aesthetics of the 1980s - it should be impossible to read any lesbian subtext at all into them at all. Fortunately for those commentators, this week's new Goliath models are a group of red-blooded men with rippling muscles and no shirts which is about as heterosexual as it gets.

The new Goliath Forge Bosses set contains six miniatures. That's broken down into two Goliaths with small bodies and a choice of weaponry; two larger Goliaths with various weapon options, probably the mini you'll pick to lead your gang; and a pair of Sump Crocs, who are basically dogs and therefore Good Boys.

1/3

I described these models as men, but that's not actually certain. The first expanded version of Goliath lore came in House of Chains, in which we learn that the Goliaths were originally created as an all-male vat-grown slave population, but that in the centuries since their creation (and after several revolutions to get control of the chems and tech they need to sustain their population) Goliath females have emerged, and there's a small population of "nat-born" Goliaths conceived the old fashioned way. It's possible that some of these bruisers could be women - perhaps the ones wearing breast plates?

The new Goliath minis will release alongside a short new supplement, 'Underhive Journal: Goliath - House of Chains'. This won't be a necessary purchase if you want to field a Goliath gang, but according to the WarCom website it will include rules for two variant gangs, the "Furnace Brutes, who are often deployed to forcefully claim territory from another house, and Unborn, which consist of those who, for whatever reason, have decided to become a Goliath artificially, with the help of a Doc".

When I say that some of the models, images, stories, and texts that make up Necromunda are queer-coded, I don't mean that you should interpret the setting as being full of queer characters. I mean that the media presents things which resonate with LGBTQ+ experiences, desires, ways of being, and so on. Many of those things overlap with heterosexual experiences - it is perfectly heterosexual to enjoy the greatest handshake in cinema, for example, but you might enjoy it for gay reasons as well.

The reason for looking at media through a specific lens - which could be a queer lens, but could be any viewpoint you care to think of - is not to try and prove that one way of seeing things is more true than any other. It's because taking different viewpoints can highlight things you might find interesting, increase your enjoyment or appreciation of a piece of work, and helps practise empathy.

Take the Goliaths. Looking at them through a queer theory lens, I see that their hyper-masculine design also resembles the gay 'muscle daddy' beauty archetype: the fact that there's no question that these guys are stone cold killers becomes a reminder that "gay" doesn't mean "weak" or "feminine". It's a duality reminiscent of the gay steel mill workers from the classic Simpson's episode 'Homer's Phobia'.

The closest real-world equivalent to the Goliath 'Unborn', who undergo medical treatment to become more muscular and more masculine is female to male gender transition: that parallel in turn complicates the idea that "gender transition" is fundamentally different in kind from other forms of bodily transformation.

Look at the Goliaths through a feminist lens and their reproduction becomes a major interest. The reality of reproduction shapes women's experience of the entire world, from the political domain to the personal, but vat-growth technology could decouple reproduction from sex. That intersects hard with a marxist analysis (one that looks at material and economic conditions and how these feed into systems of control and processes of revolution) which emphasises how the Goliaths' ability to reproduce organically, independent of vat cloning technology owned by their masters, is fundamental to their political emancipation.

These lenses aren't answers and they're not ways to win arguments, they're ways to find questions that make the world (both fictional and real) more interesting, and make us better able to connect. You can do all of this and still enjoy all the Warhammer 40k factions on the basic level that they are badass dudes who are sick as hell.

If you made it to the end of this article and had a good time, come and say hi in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: Hobby Build Academy: Building the MS-06S Zaku II Real Type and Gundam GQuuuuuuX
content:
Welcome back dear readers to a new edition of Hobby Build Academy! We hope you've been enjoying working alongside of us as we work our way deeper and deeper into the world of hobby model building; once again I am Professor Marcy, and I'm joined by my amazing assistant Elly! This week we have 2 model builds to review and discuss: The MS-06S Zaku II Real Type, as well as the Gundam GQuuuuuuX. Last time, we talked about the various types of grades in Gundam and also how to perhaps grab a Lego set that was right for you, and during that, we ended up building these two HG kits that surprised us with the pretty big gulf in what an HG kit can ask from you in terms of complexity.

Elly's Build: The MS-06S Zaku II

Elly: When we went to the Gundam Base Pop-Up, I saw this kit and really wanted to give it a shot. I know I've said I've actually not built a model in a long time and that the last time I did was very likely not an official model, but I don't think I expected this model to be quite as challenging as it ended up being. When I really get into something, I really get into it all the way, so I'd already been researching waterslide decals, and we picked up some Micro Sol and Micro Set at our local hobby shop in anticipation of having to use them.

Marcy: I've never actually used them either, so I really didn't know much about it.

Marcy: We picked up some new nippers, and I found these clay pushers very useful for some of my metallic decals; the white part separator we picked up was VERY useful in a few spots on GQX.

Elly: Well let me tell you, they were a lot harder to use than I expected! Maybe because I was a first-timer, or maybe because this model is smaller than a RG or MG, but it took me two hobby sessions to actually get this thing built and properly stickered. I hadn't really expected to spend so much time on doing so, either, so it really threw off my weekend plans. The ironic part of all of this is that the model itself was really simple to build! I had really no problems at all getting the parts together, and the new nippers we bought did a great job of cleanly separating them all so I never really needed to file or smooth anything down.

Marcy: Yeah, I almost felt bad that you had to spend so much time on the stickers, frankly; I never expected it to take you so long to get them on. But it looks amazing all complete!

Elly: My little work station, before disaster struck.

Elly: Yeah, that's basically my main takeaway from this: if you have a model that has a lot of waterslide decals like this, you should really plan for it to take twice as long as you expect if you are putting them on. And, honestly, I think the model looks pretty bad without the stickers on. When I was looking at the model without them, it looked fine, but very "toy" like. It really doesn't have a lot of detail that makes it look very spectacular otherwise. But once I had the stickers mostly on, it really started to look impressive.

Elly: Sadly, I had my first hobbying accident while building this kit; I spilled a good amount of the Micro Sol that we had bought, and I was worried that it would ruin the build, as it ended up getting on the sticker sheet. I did lose one decal, but they give you a lot of extra ones, so honestly it didn't end up mattering that much, but boy did it make this a lot more stressful than I would have liked!

Elly: This is where I ended up stopping on day 1.

Marcy: Well, you're officially a hobbyist now; at least you spilled something clear and easy to clean, unlike the many bottles of Nuln Oil Warhammer painters have ruined models, clothes, carpets, and probably marriages with.

Elly: You're saying that too seriously for me to read that as a joke, which is concerning. Anyway, I think overall I'm very happy with how this model came out, and I really learned a lot in the process. Although putting on the waterslide decals was time consuming, I think the next time I have to do it, I'd be able to do it much faster and with more confidence.

Elly: These 3 shoulder cones were probably the hardest, and I think they came out great.

Marcy: You seemed to really have the hang of it, especially on the second day, and I've still never done them, so I may have to ask you for help when I end up with them myself! What would you give the model overall?

Elly: This panel shield gave me so much anxiety. And I have enough of that already!

Elly: I'd say that the model wasn't that difficult to build, just time consuming. I think it looks super cool built and really evokes that dangerous, slick feeling of Char's Zaku that I was hoping from the box. I also think it is interesting that the stickers made it so it felt like painting wouldn't really bring me much extra from the kit, except maybe weathering, but I don't really know much about that. For an HG kit, the stickers really seemed to greatly up the difficulty, but for a first timer like me to get it to come out so good, I think just about anyone could build this kit with some patience.

Elly: I will say the bazooka is fiddly; it just kind of rests on the model and falls off easily.

Elly: If I were to give this kit a number, I'd say I'd give it an 8/10; if you don't plan to put the waterslide decals on it, I would probably skip it and look for a different Char's Zaku kit to build, as without the decals it looks VERY simplistic and toylike. I even now can see in the pictures where some panel lining paint could go a long way, so I might touch it up with a paint pen later, but I like the posability and look, and its a great testament to my first time using these types of decals!

Marcy: Here's looking at you, Amuro.

Marcy's Build: HG Gundam GQuuuuuuX

Marcy: for me, I wanted to build the GQuuuuuuX (or GQX). I'd heard that the GQX line of models had amazing posability and articulation, as well as some very modern aesthetics that help them look great even without extra painting, so I opted for the cover model itself. Although I know GQX has a pretty mixed opinion amongst Gundam fans, I really liked what the series was trying to do, and I love Nyaan and Machu a lot.

Marcy: GQuuuuuuX mostly done. You might notice a lack of red stripes. That's because the decals all sucked.

Elly: Yeah, you have a lot of GQX Machu merch, honestly. And you're even playing her in the TCG.

Marcy: Machu rules! Shame the rest of the show happens, I guess. Anyway, I am going to start this review off by making one thing clear: My build was partially ruined by decals, although mine weren't waterglide. You see, GQX is supposed to have these red line decals that give it a lot of detail, and you can see where they're supposed to be on the box. The problem, however, is that for me, these decals just refused to adhere to the model at all, and after a few attempts, even using glue, I gave up on them completely.

Elly: I felt bad, you really seemed to be having a bad time with the model because of it.

Marcy: It was very frustrating in the moment; had I known about that ahead of time, I think I would have planned to simply pick up a red paint pen, but I'll just do that next time I'm at the hobby store. When I looked up what people had to say about the model online, I found mostly people saying the same thing happened to them, which... I guess made me feel better, sort of, in that it wasn't just me messing it up.

Marcy: The arms, torso, and head of this build were some of the most fiddly, but it all went together okay.

Marcy: Unlike Elly, I will say that I had a few sections that required filing on this build. The piece that connects the torso to the legs in particular had a piece that required quite a bit of filing to get it to fit together snugly, and once it did, it was fine, but I was a little shocked at that particular piece; if you lacked a file, it could have been very frustrating to make the build work. After the model was together, though, I have to admit I was impressed.

Elly: You really couldn't stop talking about how posable it is.

Marcy: Yeah! I had heard and read that people said the GQX models have some of the best posability so far, and it really lived up to that. I was able to basically bend the model into a ball, turn the legs and arms in various ways and positions, and it never felt like the model wouldn't, or shouldn't, move in various ways. I was also pretty surprised at the fact that the weird half-feet GQX has worked so well; the model never once toppled over or felt like it would lose balance while I was posing it.

Marcy: A very cool looking kit that captures how slick GQX really is, but marred by weird decals.

Marcy: You get 2 green plastic swords, an axe, shield, and gun to play with, as well as a the backpack that can also be posed separately. I think the amount of accessories was nice for a HG kit, and the green energy swords do look pretty slick for basically requiring no real assembly or accessorizing.

Elly: Energy sword sundayyyyy!

GQuuuuuuX overall looks and poses great, but the decals really sucked the fun out of the model for me.

Marcy: If I had to give this model a rating, I'd say that for the build quality alone, an 8/10; the decals really sucked, but they don't matter to the overall build, and I can handle that part with some red paint pens; your own mileage may vary if you luck out, but just know going in that this particular kit does have some notoriously weird decals for these red lines. The other decals were great, I had no problems with them, and they were easy to get on and looked real nice easily; it was just the red line detail ones that sucked a lot of the fun out of the model build.

For HGs, this is a great kit for people who like to pose and play with models. I hear the entire GQX line is like this, so I am curious to check them out.

Wrap-Up and What We Learned

Both models presented some interesting challenges; the Zaku certainly provided the most challenge as it was our first time using waterslide decals, micro sol and micro set, but overall there weren't many problems actually building the model and getting it completed. The GQX was a similarly smooth build, but it had a few sections that required heavy filing and the decals really made for a bit of a problem in the overall build vibes. For being a modern kit, though, I think the GQX is a great kit to show how far HG models have come and how easily you can make a great looking kit at a smaller scale.

If you're a Gundam fan that wants a good piece that comes with the price of decal usage, the Zaku kit is great; as for GQX, while I like it and enjoy it now that it is built, I think the attraction factor of the kit mostly lies in whether or not you enjoy GQuuuuuX; since I'm a fan, it was an easy pick up, but if you haven't seen it or didn't like the show, this one's probably not going to be high on most people's build priorities; if you do want to give it a shot, though, I'm going to be real curious to know how you fare with the decals in your box!

Have any other questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
