content:
Although it’s a big internet out there, the Tabletop digital universe is pretty small and spread out. In Content We Liked, we take a look at the articles, videos, podcasts, and products that caught our eyes or were noteworthy during the prior week you might have missed.

On the Internet at Large

Vampiric Mechanicus by natman82

Welcome back to Content We Liked! It's been another blistering week and we’ve got some equally scorching hot hobby goodness to show you this week starting with CWL allstar natman82’s Vampiric Mechanicus, showcased here with some Nosferatu-esque Myrmidons. This is such a bonkers idea but as usual, natman makes it work by fully committing to the bit, not just gluing on some Vampire heads and calling it a day, but incorporating in that distinctive Warhammer Vampire armour designs, Zombie heads for servoskulls, and all sorts of small bloodsucking flourishes. These guys look like they’d be shambling around the pages of Requiem and that owns a whole lot.

Tomb King Chariot Crash by chogoris

Another conversion skids into our second slot this week, with a very dramatic chariot accident modeled by chogoris on Instagram. For such a simple piece of repositioning and pinning into place, this piece really nails some slow-mo dynamism that breathes a whole lotta life into a kit that’s downright ancient by miniature kit standards at this point. The verdigris stained copper deserves a shoutout as well, lending this figure a distinctive look away from the typical Tomb King schemes.

Teletext Propagandist by edpaintskrieg

Our final piece this week is bound to bring a certain misty-eyed nostalgia to Brits of a certain, rapidly aging demographic. edpaintskrieg over on Bluesky wanted their Necromunda Propagandist hanger-on to have something a little reliable to be hefting around, and boy did he get it with an Imperial reskin of the now defunct British Ceefax service freehanded on his display screens. This small detail gives so much cheeky charm, very much something you’d see painted onto a figure in White Dwarf back in Teletext’s heyday. Banger.

This Week on Tabletop Battles

Bloodbowl and The Old World brought out  the big boys this week, with revamped plastic kits of some iconic Bloodbowl Big Guy players and a new plastic Chaos Dragon gracing our review desk. We’ve also got guides to converting and painting up some of the less squeaky-clean Imperial Guard regiments, a rundown of Mandalorian Lore for Star Wars Legion, and a practical guide to getting started with the Gundam TCG.

title: Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame: The Winners of 2014, and Class of 2015
content:
The Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame is Tabletop Battles’s long-term, reader-participation initiative to recognize those novels that have “cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance” to the Black Library. Through the votes of readers as well as our community panel of community voices, we’ll examine the entire history of the Black Library, induct the latest winners, and vote for the next round’s candidates every other week.

The End Times are upon us, as we continue to see the end of Warhammer Fantasy. Surely more bitter than sweet for most, there nevertheless have been a number of stories well-remembered by the voters as we induct more Fantasy this week than any other setting.

As a reminder, if you're really enjoying this project and want to see it from a different angle, the companion piece, The Hall Monitor, runs over at my Substack, The Warhammer Wordforge. A cross between a director's commentary and behind-the-scenes look, each installment we dive a little deeper into a particular element of the Readers' Hall of Fame project. Hope to see you there!

The Envelope Please

Now, let's get to the stars of the show, the six books inducted for 2014!

Michael, Track of Words: "This is definitely not for those looking for straight-up Space Marine bolter action, although there certainly is plenty of visceral action to be found. It’s much more of a thriller, bound up in mystery and intrigue and slowly unfolding over the course of its three-part structure. As well-written as any Black Library book across the canon, it’s a brilliant follow-up to Exile, French managing to raise his game and produce a truly exceptional book mixing all of the usual Black Library elements with a compelling flair for the mysteries of the warp and this tragic cast of characters."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and Warhammer Wordforge: "Follow-up books in a series have a higher hurdle to clear. Often bereft of the novelty that saw their establishing book draw acclaim and Hall of Fame consideration, it typically takes an author willing to push the boundaries out and try something different to stand on their own. John French delivers that here, graduating from the character-in-hiding portrait we saw with Ahriman: Exile into a kind of heist story. Weaving in the tragedy of the Thousand Sons and the perils of hubris, its treatment of the Chaos legions as multidimensional beings instead of simple villains has set it apart as something truly special on its own."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and Warhammer Wordforge: "The definitive 'fall to Chaos' story of the setting, Rob Sanders penned the foundational origin story for Fantasy' preeminent villain. Deviating from being a mere caricature of evil, Sanders' tale has drawn acclaim for its more theological approach to Archaeon's gradual corruption. Despite a somewhat formulaic, quest-centered narrative arc, it's the depth of character- of this character in particular- that sees it ensconced in the Hall.

Jay, Tabletop Battles and Warhammer Wordforge: "The End Times was almost certainly the most controversial publishing event of the Black Library in its history, bringing a swift- and often abrupt- ending to a very storied property. Like a diamond formed from pressurized coal, a few exceptional stories managed to emerge from the ruin and wreckage. Chris Wraight's The Fall of Altdorf was one of the very best of the series, filled with the tragedy and despair that came from the ill-fated last stand of the Empire. Historically and aesthetically, this one's a lock."

Michael, Track of Words: "A grand, epic story, even without looking at wider events. As the forces of Chaos move through the Empire we see through the eyes of characters from both sides, some old favourites and some new introductions. In a clear sign of the changing face of Warhammer, this book very much looks at unexpected alliances, changing power structures and events with truly apocalyptic consequences; even the most powerful or well-loved characters are at risk. Wraight is clearly a safe pair of hands when it comes to this kind of story, not just because of his experience writing for the Empire but also his ability to draw strong, nuanced characters, and pull together a wide range of plot strands."

Michael, Track of Words: "The problem of scale notwithstanding, there is plenty to enjoy here. Reynolds sets the story up well before keeping events ticking along at a good pace, rotating chapters for each viewpoint character and gradually bringing (more or less) everything together towards the end for a satisfying finale. This kind of tie-in story runs the risk of being predictable, but while there is a certain sense of inevitability (given its title, and the fact that this is the End Times), there is enough plotting, backstabbing and infighting among the assembled undead to keep things interesting."

AJ, The Paladin Journal: "There are novels in the Horus Heresy series that have absolutely surpassed all expectations for me. This holds especially true for legions which had been out of the limelight by the time that this novel was released, with only a novella to tide us over. By the Emperor, what a novel though. Charting the absolute schism within the legion brought about by Horus’ civil war, it is undoubtedly one of the best in the series and it placed Chris Wraight firmly on the map as a masterful storyteller. He gave the White Scars everything they needed to be an absolute force and rewarded the fans with great characterizations, great legion culture, and a superb heartbreak story that stands out from all the other legion schism stories we’ve already seen."

Michael, Track of Words: "It’s a masterclass in character building as Wraight single-handedly turns the Scars from an unknown quantity into a legion with both a well-developed identity and a fascinating role to play in upcoming events. Their headstrong, elusive nature is what makes them so interesting, setting them apart from the other more clearly-defined legions and giving them a sense of ambiguity previously reserved for the Alpha Legion or Thousand Sons.

"It’s not just a novel-length origin story, mind – this is a beautifully plotted book full of tension and very much aware of its place within the wider series, the various strands and plot arcs all leading up to a single point which will determine the direction of the White Scars and set other events properly in motion. It’s impressive stuff, comfortably in the top tier of Heresy novels."

Aasa, The Warhammer Scholar: "Talon of Horus is the culmination for the work Aaron Dembski-Bowden has put into making previously vague Legion Wars into exciting postbellum epoch. What was once shattered warbands are now close to unifying into the Black Legion we know (and love!) as Horus and his Ezekarion plot their way out of the Warp. This series is fundamentally about Iskandar's journey of finding purpose after the Heresy, and he reaches his zenith as the Legion faces old enemies at the edge of Warp. The Long War has begun, as well as the Long Wait for ADB and Black Library continuing this exciting series."

Michael, Track of Words: "This is quite simply a book which deserves to be relished, to be savoured and enjoyed. Dembski-Bowden fills it with such life and detail, with tantalising links to the past and future of these characters, and the events that play such vital parts in the wider history. In time this will surely be looked back on as a crucial, seminal book for the 40k setting. As a standalone book this is without a doubt up there with the best that Black Library has ever published."

AJ, The Paladin Journal: "The post-Scouring era of the Warhammer 40k timeline is one of the most underutilized settings in the lore. We know precious little about it other than a few large brushstrokes. And so, to get a novel that charts the real origins of the Black Legion, the greatest villain faction in Warhammer 40k, is something truly special. What makes it even better is that Aaron Dembski-Bowden absolutely delivers on that promise.

"This era of his work for Black Library definitely has to be a golden time. The highlights are definitely the introspections by Abaddon and his cohorts, as well as that spectacular climax which took space marine aura-farming to a whole new level and delivers one of the most fascinating duel scenes in all of Warhammer. This novel is “all gas, no brakes” start to finish and sets up a fantastic beginning of a new trilogy."

Congratulations to all the worthy winners, and a very special welcome to first-timer Rob Sanders!

The Ballot: The Class of 2015

As noted previously, the polling issues we're experiencing here on Tabletop Battles are ongoing, so going forward we'll be using Google Forms (open poll, no need to be logged into Google).

To view the class of 2015 and cast your votes, please click here.

The Banner of Glory

Finally, here are all of the current members of the Black Library Readers' Hall of Fame.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

These new Allarus heavy Custodes lists are awesome - very difficult to screen, exceptionally punchy in melee and at range, and full of 4-wound, 2+/4++ save men that make the massed damage 3 in the meta a little bit awkward to use. For my part, I have the excellent scoring of Priority Assets (using my Chaos Spawn as early scoring and bait), and some damage units that absolutely cleave through Custodes units if they can connect.

We chatted before the game and our assessment broadly was that the match was drawish - playing Priority Assets my Emperor's Children have a slight passive score advantage, but the massive threat of heroic interventions and rapid ingresses means that it is very difficult for me to push into the Custodes, who get to work their way into the game and then push me.

This is very much how the first few turns of the game played out - I use my outer layer of Spawn and chaff to screen any nasty Allarus Ingresses, whilst picking off Custodes units where I was able. In turn Adam threatened Fight on Death and Intervention wherever he could to keep a secure hold on his expansion and begin to threaten mine.

In the end, we both maxed Primary with Adam winning narrowly on Secondaries. We identified that there was a moment in 3-4 where I mismanaged the screen of some Allarus after a Lord Exultant suddenly bombed a ten inch charge I hadn't been expecting him to make. This created too many engagements and allowed the Allarus to get up the board a turn early, which hurt my ability to keep them back and gave Adam a couple of cards he probably would have struggled to get otherwise. I'd played a very good passive game early on, but I needed to evolve that into pushing back at Adam more decisively in the mid to late game - getting this wrong ultimately saw me come out the wrong side of the draw, 93-97.

Adam was a brilliant opponent, and the game was collaborative, intense and hard fought, exactly like a final should be. Congratulations on your victory!!

Thoughts

This one's got video! You can see the stream from Wargames Live here:

We've talked a lot about Darkflight this week but now you get to see them in action in a game where they actually lose. Which isn't quite what Jeremy wants broadcast, but them's the breaks. Darkflight lists tend to do a great job controlling the tempo, picking of units that stray too far afield while staying out of range of the rest of the opponent's army. By keeping an opponent from interacting with anything on turns 1/2, they can control the pace of the game and scoring and force opponents to engage on their terms.

In this particular game, Jeremy's fatal mistake was getting a bit too aggressive - he put the Land Speeder Vengeance a bit too far forward, then repeated the mistake with the Lion and Azrael. The turn 2 Vengeance loss was the start of a snowball effect, giving the Emperor's Children player Bring it Down and extra forward movement while pushing the Lion too far forward opened him him up to a charge that removed him pretty quickly - Frenzied Host is a big help going into the Lion as it gives the Infractors S5 on their attacks on the charge, doubling their expecting output with their Duelling Sabres. This is more or less only possible with the changes to Fights First in 11th edition, and once the Lion goes down, Azrael is more or less undefended. Likewise, the Daemonettes removing Azrael and the Defiler taking out the Inner Circle Companions essentially left Jeremy without much in the way of strong melee pieces on turn 3, capping off a huge turn that ended up being the backbreaker.

If you've never played against the Carnival of Excess Defiler, count yourself lucky. The Reaper Autocannons on the EC Defiler come with [SUSTAINED HITS 1] built-in, making them one of the few units in the army which can immediately benefit from the 5+ crits. So your Defilers hit on 2+ against targets above half strength with Sustained Hits 1 and crits on 5+. I slept on these and then one shot Magnus to death in one activation. Don't let it happen to you.

title: Getting Started With Trickcal: Chibi Go
content:
Longtime readers of the site probably know that I play a lot of games; I’ve spent a good majority of my life playing them, writing about them, thinking about them, and occasionally working on them. I’ve spent over a year on this very Website writing about Umamusume: Pretty Derby, and there are a lot of games I regularly play and enjoy that I love the thought of sharing with others; particularly, I think the mobile/phone/tablet gaming scene has a lot of wheat to separate from chaff, with a lot of really great games that exist in an ecosystem that isn’t always easy to discern, discover, or frankly trust. Earlier this year, I happened to see a particular little creature show up a lot on my various socials: Bluesky, Xiaohongshu, Instagram, YouTube, everywhere I looked I kept seeing this cute, pathetic sort of… thing.

This thing.

I had to know what it was, where it came from, and why it kept yelling “좋아요” (Joayo/Cuayo), and that’s how I discovered a game that has ever since occupied a constant place in my mind. I love this game, I think more people should love this game, and hopefully I can convince you to give it a try. That game? Trickcal: Chibi Go, a creation of Epid Games and published by Bili Bili for Android and iOS platforms, is a charming, silly, fun, and surprisingly thoughtful world that sucks you in with cute chibi characters and goofy mechanics like being able to pull their cheeks (even during cutscenes), delivers a surprisingly deep auto-battler system that actually seems to know how to “auto”, and the part that has kept me around: one of the best worlds I’ve seen built and realized in a game lately.

We’re On A Mission From God

As Master of the Order, you have a house, and lots of devoted followers. Who are all weird.

Let me start with that world building before getting into how to play the game and what I find so enjoyable about it. In Trickcal, players take on the role of The Master (교주 or Gyoshu in Korean,which can be read as either “cult leader” or “religious leader”), a faceless and genderless stand-in character that you get to name when you start the game. There really isn’t anything known about “Gyoshu” except that they are from Earth and have somehow found themselves in the world called Elias, inhabited by various races: Sprites, Witches, Werebeasts, Phantoms, Dragons, Elementals, and Elves, who also come from outside of Elias (and have a lot of trauma about Earth and Santa). Gyoshu really has no powers, special abilities, or superheroic abilities, but they do have a few things to their name: human reasoning, size, and a gun.

Ner (left) is the long suffering advisor to Erpin (right) who only really wants to eat bread. Or literally anything, frankly.

Your immediate introduction to the world of Elias come as the Sprite kingdom is leading a rebellion against the gluttonous and dim-witted Queen, Erpin, and her long-suffering advisor and leader of the Church of Yggdrasil, Ner. I was mostly just along for the ride to check the game out when the initial prologue started talking about multi-level-marketing schemes and debating whether insects that are squashed go to the “Weekend Ranch” or “Weekend Farm”, establishing that Elias (apparently) has no concept of death. I’m going to level with you, dear reader: this made me bust out laughing at how stupid the conversation became, and from there, I ended up finding myself hooked.

Everyone in this story is some form of a moron, but endearingly. This is Pyrrha, a dragon who makes fake gold, because... she's the Pyrite Dragon, so she's also a loan shark. Of course.

Trickcal is a testament to worldbuilding, frankly, and perhaps the somewhat complicated history of Trickcal: Chibi Go’s development is part of that reason. There was a webnovel called “The Trickcal” which predated any games, and another game called “Trickcal” which shut down very early in service; Trickcal: Chibi Go is functionally the third attempt to bring the concept to life, and a lot of that development shows in just how fully realized the characters and world they inhabit are. I mostly expected the game to be silly, and it is, comically so, but the more I played the more I was pulled into the mystery and charm of the game: Yggdrasil is sick, dying, or possibly already dead, there are numerous threats to Elias and its relative peace, and somehow Gyoshu finds themselves at the center of all of it. As players meet various characters, play through their stories, and experience the new events that expand on the story, I also found that Trickcal does something that I have criticized other mobile games for in the past: it has not just horizontal depth of constant updates, but it has vertical depth, as characters change, impact the story, and the story does not simply forget their existence the moment someone more popular or interesting is introduced.

The writing in this game is honestly so funny at times it catches me off guard.

I know that sounds like odd praise, perhaps, if you’re not overly familiar with mobile games, but Trickcal’s uses of foreshadowing, character depth, and urging players to remember even very small details as the story develops makes Elias feel like an actual world that you’re interacting with, rather than a simple power fantasy where your character solves all problems and nothing is ever at stake. Perhaps my favorite example of this are the mysterious “Eldynes”, a group of 7 sisters who all seem to be separated by some event players are unaware of, and their slow meetings through the story provide a lot of flavor and strife as simply being sisters doesn’t mean they’ll reconnect or get along, let alone recognize one another; without going too far into spoiling the story events, the interactions of the Eldyne sisters alone makes for compelling and at times heartwrenching drama in a game that seems like it should just be silly on the surface.

Set Expectations to Whimsy

Trickcal is nothing if not colorful.

That balance in narrative that Trickcal strikes is maybe the best part of its whimsical nature: it loves to go for laugh out loud jokes and situations, while also tempering those with emotional stakes and character growth that the player is not actually all that relevant to solving; something else I loved about the game is that Gyoshu exists, but is not the character present in every story or event, perhaps even explicitly to the detriment of what is going on: without the presence of a “wise outsider” like in a lot of games, things can and do go wrong, leaving the pieces to be solved… maybe.

Trickcal has one consistent message: ACAB.

That isn’t to say that every event is depressing or ends badly; a lot of them are silly, too, and the whimsy of Trickcal is the thing that keeps me coming back to it. I love the art design, the cute characters, the colorful world, the little references and attention to detail that are worked into the game; the developers at Epid have a big love for cinema, mythology, and literature that shows up in surprising ways. Even the aforementioned cheek pinching mechanic just seems completely silly, and the sudden proliferation of Speaki into defacto mascot of the game just fits in with the cute and relaxing vibe the game wants to give off, which it then counterbalances with the deeper narrative aspects and developments.

Epid really loves little cute references, such as this Breaking Bad one.

The Global version of the game, which is the one I’m playing, is quite a bit behind the Korean version of the game, which also gives me a little foresight into what is coming down the pipe, and almost everything I ever hear about from Korean friends playing the game is that the best is yet to come, which is… oddly exciting? So many games that have development/release gaps often go through cycles of “oh you’ll hate this”, such as Umamusume’s community maligned Trackblazer era. All I ever hear about Trickcal is excitement on excitement for the next story, the next bits of character development and progress, and even the bits I don’t fully understand but hear about have me curious; the game successfully sucks you in if you let it, and I’ve not regretted a single second spent with the characters and world.

Elves can't catch a break, even in Elias.

But how does it play? Well…!

Accepting the Mantle of Leadership

Trickcal is an auto-battler, in the sense that players do not control every single aspect of combat in a game. You select certain upgrades and developments mid-battle, set your teams up pre-battle, and can control the use of various skills and abilities during the course of a battle, but otherwise your chibis will do all of the fighting for you. At times auto-battlers tend to carry the stigma of being simple or boring, games that play themselves, but I find that Trickcal really seems to show that isn’t the case. There are numerous ways in which the game wants your input and strategizing, while also allowing you to take a backseat during farming or routine sorts of maintenance style tasks you might do while playing.

Generally, you'll make teams of 6, like this.

Teams are traditionally built of 6 characters, although some modes allow for 9, which are usually boss raids that can be fairly hectic and “end game” in their challenge. Team building rewards utilizing various characters of the same “Emotion”, or color, ranging from Purple (Depressed), Yellow (Vivacious), Innocent (Green), Composed (Blue) and Madness (Red). One of the more interesting wrinkles is seeing how these various Emotions manifest in the way the characters themselves act or behave; there are certainly characters you’ll encounter who don’t seem all that Composed, and others who you wouldn’t believe are “Mad” (read: angry), but…let’s just say that part is flavor.

Sometimes, you'll even make teams of 9!

The more of each type you have in a party, the bigger the bonuses are that you get, working in pairs: 2, 4, 6, in increasing bonuses. Mixed teams are also possible, such as 2/4, or in Raid style content, 2/4/2/1, 4/4/1, 2/2/2/1, and so forth. Generally, though, you’ll want to focus on trying to build teams of single Emotions to get the biggest buffs. If you’re a brand new player who intends to pick the game up from reading this: Pick a single Emotion and build that team, with Depressed being one of the best teams to build around, especially if you obtain the character Yomi. The bonuses are fairly easy to understand, in that 2 of a type gives 6%, 4 gives 28%, and 6 gives a whopping 66% increase to HP and Damage. Even just running 4 of a single Emotion can go a long way to allowing a newer player to make their way through difficult content as they build their roster and overall collection of Apostles to work under them.

Your Apostles need skills, gear, and crayons to be their best selves.

I’ll take this time to mention that Trickcal: Chibi Go is a gacha game, in that the characters, cards (equipment and runes) are pulled from corresponding banners that refresh regularly. I know that many people have complicated feelings towards gacha games and mechanics, so I wanted to take a moment to explain how Trickcal’s works: after pulling 200 times (150 for cards) on an Apostle banner, players can cash in to obtain the Apostle; the only difference here are Eldynes, who are generally more powerful characters that are occasionally added to the game and require 300 to “cash in”; that pity system carries over from banner to banner, and is one of the more generous versions of this mechanic I’ve seen. I will ALSO say that the Trickcal banner rates can be a little brutal, so perhaps that’s balanced out by the ability to store up.

Clearing challenging content like Dreamworlds isn't even that hard, nor does it take a "deluxe" team!

Generally, though, I have found Trickcal is one of the most Free To Play (F2P) friendly games I’ve ever played. The developers give out free 3 star character items like literal candy, characters can be farmed from 2 different dungeons, and generally there’s no direct benefit to pulling numerous copies of a character for someone who isn’t overly interested in min-maxing characters; Epid’s CEO has mentioned he mostly wants people to enjoy the world of Trickcal, and it shows, because even finding reasons to give the game money can be difficult, frankly. Pulling doesn’t reward reckless spending, materials are never scarce, and skins are about the only thing that exists to make your game “prettier”, being totally optional. That doesn’t  mean the game does not have micro-transactions or gacha, though, so if those are inherently deal breakers, I don’t know if Trickcal: Chibi Go will change your mind on that, which is a totally valid position to take.

Exploring Elias

If you do decide to make the plunge and check out the game, there’s a lot to do, and yet also all the time in the world to do it. A “daily” session of Trickcal at bare minimum can take about 10 minutes maximum, but if you’re reading the stories and doing other aspects, you basically can play as much as you want and do whatever you want in it, in various increments. The main battle part of the game is available through “Crusade”, which includes various difficulties and scaling difficulty to test your team against, and also presents you the best way to procure various equipment materials for your Apostles. Dungeons offers various ways to get specific resources, like money, upgrade materials, Apostle certificates, and much more. There’s PVP, a rotating set of Raid style events (Dimension Clash and Elias Frontier), and 2 separate daily challenges; frankly, there’s almost too MUCH to do in the game.

I said it was consistent.

This doesn’t even account for the various stories: the main story itself, apostle stories, event stories, and one of the things I enjoy is that past events are added fairly quickly to the game, meaning that you can catch up on character stories you may have missed and events you didn’t get to play without a hassle or some sort of obtuse system; Events are added a few patches after they initially ran, but last I checked there are only a few missing since I started playing that have not yet made it to the theater to watch.

Events and Apostle stories let you get to know them better, such as Kommy's political beliefs. (based)

There’s also events that run for a few weeks, generally to introduce new characters to the game/story. Some are characters that haven’t made their full appearance or had their own time in the spotlight, and others are stories that help flesh out a character in more detail by showing how they interact with the world around them; as I said above, the world building is excellent and rewarding, and the character gimmicks are often hilarious and charming, like xXionx, a self-aware cringelord failwoman with a heart of gold, ED, who thinks the world around her is a gigantic lucid dream, Shoupan, a delivery person who hates cops as much as she hates going slow, and Kyarot, a somewhat clueless farmer who loves her plants to the point of committing violent crimes in their defense. I have to give the game credit in that I can’t say I can (yet) think of a single character I dislike, as antagonistic characters are often fleshed out to have more depth than you’d expect.

Trickcal Chibi Go to the Polls

I could honestly talk about the game more, but that would probably be beating a dead horse at this point; I’ll simply say that I love this game a lot, and I really do hope you’ll consider giving it a try. It is currently available on iOS and Android devices, but there’s no PC client yet; there are some ways you can try to play it on Android emulation like MuMu, and I’ve had some success with doing so (many of the screenshots you see here were taken using MuMu, actually). Recommending games can often be a bit of a gamble, because talking about how much you love something doesn’t always mean you can convince people to take the plunge with you, and in the event that it isn’t their thing, well, at least you tried.

Again, the amount of times this game says out of pocket things that make me laugh is pretty regular.

Trickcal’s colorful and cute whimsy is what sold it to me, and it has a very vibrant and fun community that love the game across the globe; one of the fun parts of the Speaki explosion is also the vast amount of creativity I’ve seen for the game, and perhaps it’s just relaxing to see a game that people from various parts of the world all enjoy together and share how much they love the game with one another; I am not trying to say that Trickcal is going to solve global political relations, but it does at least feel nice to occasionally see something bring people together instead of set them at one another’s throats.

xXionx describing your average discord server.

If you do end up trying the game, don’t fret if some of it seems overwhelming; I plan on revisiting the game and talking about how to build teams, challenge various difficult aspects of the raid systems, and more in the future, and maybe I’ll even see some of you around in the game! Until then, keep your Apostles well fed on candy and cake, and I hope you have even half as much fun in Elias as I do!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Arcane Journal March of Chaos
content:
Hello my beautiful Old Worlders! Hot on the heels of the release of a new Core Rulebook and a big confusing FAQ, Games Workshop drops a new Arcane Journal with all of the seasonings we need to spice up our games with a new (completely optional but Matched Play legal) upgrade to Magic, a plethora of 'corrupted' core magic items available to every faction in the game (except Dwarves because they're not allowed to have nice things), and a brand new Army of Infamy for the Forces of Chaos allowing you to mix and match a portion of your Warriors of Chaos and Beastmen army collections.

With the forces of the dark gods converging on the lands of elves and men both sides are pulling out all the stops, so let's dive in and let the chaos begin

A New Way To Make The Magic Happen

The first big reveal in the March of Chaos is the return of the Winds of Magic. In previous editions of Warhammer Fantasy Battle, the Winds of Magic were a dice pool that was generated by each player every turn and it was those dice that players would use to cast and dispel spells. It is a part of the game that at least I personally miss when compared to how magic is handled in the Old World so color me happy that it is kind of coming back. In the before times while some rounds were just determined by who was able to toss the most dice at any given spell, many more were layered and deeply strategic. While these new Winds of Magic rules are not all of that, they do add a new layer of interactivity to your games that I've been excited to see play out.

The Winds of Magic in March of Chaos can be played in one of two ways; either Arcane Magic or Channeling. Games electing to use Arcane Magic gain access to the all new Arcane Ploy deck (available to purchase from your Local Game Store or Papa James themselves). During your pre-game setup, both players draw 6 arcane ploy cards from their deck or, if they do not have access to a deck, roll 6 times on the chart provided in the Arcane Journal to generate them. These ploys can be used by any unit in your army that can cast or dispel spells or use bound spells making them extremely powerful additions to your respective magic 'phases'.

There are 11 different Arcane Ploys to choose from with a range of strengths, though the most powerful are limited to 1-2 per player to avoid one person getting overly lucky and completely upending the game before it starts. The rarest ploys are Towering Conjuration which allows a wizard to target any unit on the board with a spell regardless of line of sight or range and Absolute Power that makes your next spell a perfect invocation on any roll of a double so long as you meet the casting cost. Other ploys grant you free rerolls on casts and dispels, toss extra dice at casting/dispelling attempts or simply automatically dispel a spell with no roll required. In general, the ploys are neat add-ons to the game but so much of the magic has been neutered these days that these only go so far to adding interest to what we already have.

If playing with a deck is a bit to random for your liking (like it is for me) then Channeling may be more appealing. Channeling grants each player pools of dice for each of the wizards/rune priests you have included in your list with higher level caster generating more dice than their weaker counterparts. Each level 1 wizard in your army generate 1d3 dice, level 2s generate 1d3+1, level 3s 2d3 and level 4s get you 2d3 +1 dice for your pool. These channeled dice can be used for 5 different effects throughout your games: A channeled die can be used to reroll a generated spell at the beginning of the game, to add an additional die to your casting and dispelling rolls (discarding the lowest), add range to a casting or dispel attempt, or 2 dice can be used to completely reroll a casting or dispel roll (except miscasts). There is no limit to how many times you use your channeled dice in your turn, other than the dice remaining in your respective casters' pools.

This is my favorite of the two ways to play the Winds of Magic and has been a novel addition in the small handful of games I've gotten to try it. The abilities granted by the dice are just enough to make things interesting. Especially because of the downsides. Did I mention using the Winds of Magic has a downside? Because it does and it is wild. Should you and your opponent choose to add the Winds of Magic to your game, you have to also use the all new, extremely punishing, Disastrous Miscast table rather than the old Kinda Meh Miscast table that is sometimes actually good for you. Disastrous Miscasts are extremely punishing, with effects reminiscent of the old 8th edition miscasts amped up to 11. Results on this table range from Str 10 AP 4 flame templates launching out of the wizards belly before it gets sucked into the void and being immediately killed, to being permanently reduced to lvl 1 or having your casting and dispelling rolls reduced by 1 or more for the remainder of the game. Just an absolute bundle of fun that I highly recommend. Having my little spellweaver try to dispel an enemy's attempt at hammerhand only to vomit pure unadulterated violence onto the offending unit before being deleted by the gods was a glorious thing to behold.

The New Winds of Magic make even the lowliest wizards a potential threat. Until they get bodied by the void. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Whether you choose to play Channeling or Arcane Magic, the book also opens up another addendum to magic use in the Old World; Sorcerous Ruses. These are 25 point, random, single-use 'special abilities' (they do not take up any magic item allotment) that give your wizards access to potentially powerful effects...if they go off. If you are addicted to the lottery effect, Sorcerous Ruses are for you. For every wizard that you choose to purchase a Sorcerous Ruse for you roll a d6 at the beginning of the game and gain a special triggered ability. Escapology brings a wizard that just died back to life with 1 wound remaining on a 4+ dice roll, while the remaining 5 Ruses are special dispel effects with potentially big upsides. Daemonic Assailants, for example, has your wizard roll a d6 and add their wizard level while your opponent must roll a d6 and add their wizard's toughness. Should the results be equal, you simply dispel the spell, should your roll be greater, the dispel is dispelled and the caster suffers a single wound with no saves of any kind allowed. Spell Eater is by far the strongest possible ruse, automatically dispelling an opponent's spell or  letting you attempt to dispel a perfect invocation AND the next time your wizard casts a spell they may choose to cast the spell they ate the previous turn with an extra D6 added to the roll. While cute, I wish there were a few more Ruses options that were not just variants on dispels and the randomness factor probably means Ruses see little competitive play. Still, I don't believe they are particularly game-breaking and I'm always a fan of adding new options to your games.

You...Are...Cursed

In addition to the newly upgraded ways of wizardry, March of Chaos adds 17 new 'corrupted' core magic items to the game that, as stated previously, can be used by any faction that isn't stunty. As always, while most of the items here are more narratively focused than useful particularly given how they all have negative effects built in, there are a handful here that will definitely see play in the highest levels of play, including one of the best weapons we've seen to date.

Of particular note and in no particular order:

Daemon-Blooded Steed is a very good Enchanted Item that I imagine Warriors of Chaos and Wood Elf players will try to slot into their lists as it grants cavalry mounts +1 movement, strength and attacks. This is a sweet perk for the recently buffed Daemonic Mounts and Great Stags at the minor cost of gaining the Impetuous rule.

The Amulet of Spell Attraction is a new 25 point talisman that savvy players can employ to gain further control of their opponents' magic phases. Once per turn, the wielder may make a Leadership test when a friendly unit within their command range is targeted by a Magic Missile or Hex and if the roll is successful they may have the spell redirected to them instead. Given that this happens during targeting, you can do some really interesting things here, most obviously forcing your opponents biggest/scariest spell onto a unit with high Magic Resistance or just severely limiting a 'go' turn by forcing a devastating hex onto an unchargeable or hidden target.

The Flail Of Wrecks is an incredibly strong weapon at 45 points. As a flail, it grants the user Str +2 and Armourbane(1) on any turn it charged and always has an AP value of -2. Additionally and most importantly it has the Multiple Wounds (2) special rule. The only downside to the Flail is any roll of 1 to wound reduces the wielder's initiative by 1 which is a very minor annoyance, particularly on elven lords with Strikes First or Chaos Lords that are making their enemies initiative 1 anyway. This is arguably the strongest weapon in the game for the vast majority of factions and I would expect to see it everywhere.

Finally, I need to give a special nod to the Mantle of Drifting Shadow. This 20 point piece of Light Armor is for infantry only and makes its wielder untargettable by shooting or spells outside of 6 inches at the cost of gaining the Loner special rule. While being untargettable is a pretty neat effect in and of itself and would have been incredible on the Daemon Prince before it became a Monster, the Loner downside here is actually all upside for a couple of factions. Chaos players will have a field day being able to add a Sorceror Lord or BSB to a unit of Forsaken of Khorne ramping an already fantastic unit up to 11 with access to the Taskmaster Scourge, Daemonlogy spells, Brazen Collar or any number of banners and I'm sure Wood Elf players would love to be able to add a Spellweaver or Glade Lord to their units of Wardancers. As a lover of jank, I've been brewing combos for these guys for a couple of days now and absolutely been reveling in it.

The Daemon-Blooded Steed is a great upgrade for the already powerful Daemonic Mount. Credit: Falcon40k

The Hordes of Chaos

Last, and possibly least, the followers of Chaos get themselves a brand spanking new Army of Infamy and the option to create Champions of Ruin, though the latter is for narrative play only as Games Workshop are notoriously cowards.

The Hordes of Chaos army of infamy is designed to allow chaos players to mix and match units from their Warriors of Chaos and Beastmen collections into a cohesive force vying for the attention of their Gods.

As far as the composition list goes. The Hordes of Chaos allows for 1 Daemon Prince, Beast Lord, or Chaos Lord in your list regardless of points, 1 Exalted Champion, Great Bray Shaman, or Sorceror Lord per 1000 points and any number of the other character options from Ravening Hordes minus the Doombull who has been replaced by the all new Cult Magister.

Core units in Hordes must make up 33% of your list and you are forced to include at least 1 unit of Warriors of Chaos or Marauders and 1 unit of Gors or Ungors. Additionally, you may take any number of Chaos Warhounds or the new Chaos Cultists. If your army contains a Chaos Lord/Exalted Champ or Daemon Prince as your General then you may take a single unit of Chosen Chaos Warriors as Core, while if you elected to take a Beastlord then you may take a unit of Bestigors in this slot instead.

At special, we see the addition of Marauder Horsemen, Chaos Knights and Chaos Chariots. If your general is a Chaos Lord/Daemon Prince or Exalted Champ then you can also add a unit of Chosen Knights here. While at Rare (which is up to 33% instead of the normal 25) Hordes players can slot in a Shaggoth or any number of Chaos Spawn, Minotaurs, Dragon Ogres, Chimeras, Chaos Giants, Cygors or Ghorgons.

The Option to take Chosen Warriors in Core is a tantalizing one. Even if it probably isn't a particularly strong one.

Unfortunately, as you can see, a lot of faction favorites are missing from this army list. There are no Razorgors, Harpies, or Forsaken to be seen and no Gigantic Spawn or Warpfires either. The moving of all the normal core cavalry units to special is also a huge blow to list building if you're someone playing with objectives in your games. That said, there is still some combo-potential here that you can't get anywhere else and the idea of a Chosen Warrior deathstar is probably appealing to someone.

In terms of special rules, this composition list comes with four. An Unholy Union is the most powerful of the effects, though it is clear that someone got hurt somewhere along the way as the riders on it make it less appealing than it could be. Whilst within 6 inches of a friendly Beastmen unit, Warriors of Chaos units gain rerolls of 1 to hit, while Beastmen units gain rerolls of 1 to wound when within 6 of any Warriors of Chaos. In addition, while within 6 of each other, both factions may choose to apply a -1 to their Flee rolls. It must be noted that these effects are not triggered by and do not effect any characters or units that are shared by both factions in the Ravening Hordes army book. So no juicing up your Dragon Ogres or Spawn with this effect. The lack of character synergy here is the real bummer, particularly given the limited army options in the composition list. That said, rerolls are always welcome and smoothing out a combat phase for your expensive Knights or Warriors just by having a dozen ungors chilling in the back is a small price to pay.

The second special rule and the only other one with a positive effect is For the Dark Gods! Every time a character in your army kills a model in a challenge they must immediately roll on the Gaze of the Gods table and your army general gets a free reroll when using the Gaze. Free Gaze rerolls are always welcome, even if they are a 5 point upgrade option otherwise, and it is pretty common for your Chaos Lords and Champions to have to roll through multiple challenges over the course of the game. This is a pretty flavorful special rule and has the potential to turn your best combat veterans into insane blenders by the end of a game with some lucky rolls.

The final two rules for the Hordes of Chaos are Untrusting Allies and The Shadow Grows. Untrusting Allies simply states that Chaos Characters cannot join Beastmen units and vice versa and neither faction can use the leadership of a character from the other one. The Shadow Grows is a rehash of the same rule in the Heralds of Darkness army of infamy and forces you to have a rank and file unit with a specific mark of chaos for every character you have in your list that has one which further limits your army customization options though here at least it isn't as big of a loss as you'll rarely have more than 2 characters with special marks anyway.

New Units

The Hordes of Chaos introduces 2 new units exclusive to the army and both are very solid additions to your lists.

The Chaos Cultist costs 6ppm comes in squads of 5-20 and has a standard human stat-line with 3s in all the important places, 4 inches of movement and a leadership of 6 (7 with their Apostle champion in play). They come stock with extra hand weapons and throwing weapons though they may swap them for short bows should they wish for free. They come with the Open Order, Skirmishers, Warband, Mark of Chaos Undivided and Ambushers special rules in addition to Dark Pawns and Unseen Threat. Dark Pawns means that friendly units do not have to worry about panicking should a unit of friendly cultists breaks, runs through them, or explodes nearby. Unseen Threat is the real sauce here as it grants the unit a +1/-1 to their rolls to come in from Ambush AND allows them to deploy within 4 inches of enemy units when they do instead of the normal 8 which is really spicy for things like threatening baggage trains or overwhelming smaller backfield units.

The Arcane Journal recommends using a particularly spoopy looking Empire Wizard for your cult magister. Like this Amethyst Wizard absolutely force choking her uber driver offscreen. Credit: Charlie Brassley

The Cult Magister is a 55 points lvl 1 wizard that has been hitting the gym. It is an incredible stat line for its points being WS 5, Str and To 4 with 2 attacks at leadership 8 just like a Sorceror Lord. Given that for whatever reason this bozo can be equipped with a flail for just 3 more points, we're already cooking with gas. They may take a spell from the lore of Dark or Daemonology but unlike other wizards it has no option to upgrade to level 2. This is fine because The Summoning is a very good spell if you don't hit the Steed of Shadows lottery roll. The Magister may pay for ambushers for 5 points and may take up to 25 points in magic items. They have the Mark of Chaos Undivided and two unique special rules; Sacrifice and Thralls of Chaos. Thralls of Chaos simply locks Magisters to units with the Dark Pawns special rule (so just cultists for now), while Sacrifice gives every Magister a free Jagged Dagger. Every time they choose to cast a spell, the Magister can choose to kill a model in its unit and gain a bonus to their next cast equal to the wounds characteristic of the dead. I can definitely see a world where players toss a couple of Magistrates in a unit of Cultists just to sling a little more murder from afar, something the Warriors of Chaos generally lack.

Sample List: Just Chosen Stuff

382 - Chaos Lord, Shield, Mark of Nurgle, Extra Arm, General, Daemonic Mount, Flail of Wrecks, Daemon-Blooded Steed, Crown of Everlasting Conquest

175 - Aspiring Champion, Flail, Shield, Mark of Chaos Undivided, Battle Standard Bearer, Monster Hunter's Tapestry, Talisman of the Carrion Crow

300 - Sorcerer Lord, Mark of Chaos Undivided, Wizard Level 4, Daemonology, Taskmaster's Scourge, Spell Familiar, Tome of the Dark Gods

58 - Cult Magister, Flail

58 - Cult Magister, Flail

498 - 18 Chosen Chaos Warriors, Full Plate Armour, Shield, Drilled, Mark of Nurgle, Enhanced Reflexes, Champion, Brazen Collar, Standard Bearer, War Banner, Musician

72 - 12 Chaos Cultists

72 - 12 Chaos Cultists, Shortbow

77 - 12 Ungor Herds, Shortbow, Ambushers, Musician

65 - 10 Ungor Herds, Shortbow, Musician

65 - 10 Ungor Herds, Shortbow, Musician

198 - 3 Dragon Ogres, Heavy Armour, Great Weapon

Here's a quick and dirty list that's far from optimized but tries its damnedest to make Chosen Warriors a thing while holding to the max 25% of your army rule for any individual unit. The goal here is pretty simple, BSB and Sorceror Lord join the Chosen Warriors, hope you get Steed of Shadows and then abuse it and drilled along with the fleet-footed and ambushing Ungors giving them rerolls to bully opponents with a flying wall of heavily armored meat. Your Chaos Lord's job is to be an ICBM and your Dragon Ogres keep your opponents honest when they try to flank your beautiful chosen boys and girls. The Magisters join the Cultist unit with the shortbows to fling a handful of arrows and the summoning spells at lighter targets while the Cultists with throwing weapons and extra hand weapons hunt war machines and baggage trains.

Thoughts

The March of Chaos is certainly an interesting Arcane Journal with a number of welcome additions to the game that may just reinvigorate folks that have been at this since launch. The new Winds of Magic effects are a fun addition that I hope at least occasionally get picked up for tournament play and the new magic items may actually shake up the meta in some form or another which I'm always grateful for. The only real downer here is the Hordes of Chaos army of infamy, though I can understand why everything about it seems reined in to one degree or another as it is definitely an idea that can get out of hand fast. That said, in trying to work through army lists for the faction I find myself really annoyed by all the restrictions and the actual lack of synergy when trying to put together something with a bit of optimization or even with just a good mix of Beasts and Warriors. This may also be because of the recent nerfs to Hagtree and Viletide make Great Brays a lot more disappointing an option. This AoI would have gotten a big shot in the arm for me if at least razorgors and harpies had been options as right now I find it hard to slot in anything more than a handful of ungors into my lists.

Regardless, I think Old World players should be stoked about what we've gotten here, the whole package gets a solid B+ from me.

title: Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Brings Slavic & Balkan Folklore to Life in a New Fantasy TTRPG Setting
content:
Eren Chronicles has launched Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch, a new tabletop role-playing game setting inspired by Slavic and Balkan folklore, on Kickstarter. The campaign, which went live on Tuesday, has already surpassed $120,000 in funding within its first day, making it one of the most notable Dungeons & Dragons 5e campaigns of the year.

Zamanora transports players and Dungeon Masters into a world of rural communities, dark forests, and vengeful witches. The setting is designed to support both Wizards of the Coast’s Dungeons & Dragons 5e and 2024 editions, as well as Legend In The Mist, the rustic fantasy RPG from Son of Oak Game Studio that was recently voted the Most Anticipated TTRPG of 2025.

The Zamanora setting draws heavily from Slavic and Balkan folklore, offering players a chance to explore a world where cautionary tales come to life. Players can create characters from fantastical local creatures such as the mischievous Chorts and the spectral Huants. The setting also introduces unique subclasses, including the Bogatyr fighter, Guslar bard, and Hearth-domain cleric, allowing for thematic storytelling deeply tied to the region’s traditions.

Two new magic systems are introduced in Zamanora: Poppet Magic, a manipulative form of spellcasting, and Ceremonial Magic, which enables non-casters to perform magical rituals. These systems provide fresh ways for players to engage with the game world.

The setting features a variety of mythical creatures familiar to fans of Slavic and Balkan folklore, such as the leshy, baba yaga, and kikimora. These beings are joined by a host of other monsters, each accompanied by detailed descriptions and lore.

The Zamanora Kickstarter offers a range of rewards for backers, from digital PDFs to deluxe collector’s editions. Pledge tiers include options for digital content, physical books, and various accessories. The Core, Deluxe, and Collector’s Boxes include items such as dice, a GMless adventure deck, Baba Yaga miniatures, a DM screen, a monster deck, an illustrated slipcase, and a hand-knitted plushie.

A free demo of the Zamanora setting is available for download on the Kickstarter page, allowing potential backers to explore the world before committing to a pledge.

For more information or to support the project, visit the Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Kickstarter page.

title: Mantic Games Teases New Fantasy Wargame: Kings of War: Champions

title: New Reinforcements Arrive in Infinity: PanOceania, Yu Jing, Shindenbutai, and Nomads Expand Their Forces
content:
Corvus Belli has introduced a series of new units and expansion packs for its tabletop game, Infinity, bringing additional options to the PanOceania, Yu Jing, and Shindenbutai factions, while also adding the Nomads to the mix.

Kestrel Expansion Pack Beta: PanOceania’s Colonial Forces

The Kestrel Colonial Force is featured in this expansion, showcasing PanOceania’s adaptability in addressing the challenges of space colonization. As a leading power in the Human Sphere, PanOceania leverages its resources to maintain its position, and the Kestrel forces exemplify this approach. Equipped with advanced technology, these units are designed to uphold PanOceania’s strategic interests.

White Banner Expansion Pack Beta: Yu Jing’s Strategic Elite

Yu Jing, often regarded as one of the top powers in the Human Sphere, continues to strengthen its military capabilities with the White Banner Army. This force has demonstrated its effectiveness in conflicts such as the struggle over Svalarheima. Combining cultural heritage with modern technology, the White Banner Army represents Yu Jing’s commitment to achieving its goals through disciplined and strategic action.

Shindenbutai Expansion Pack Beta: Tradition Meets Innovation

On the distant planet of Shinju, the Shindenbutai serve as the military arm of Greater Independent Japan. This force blends traditional samurai values with advanced technology, creating a unique and versatile unit. Tasked with protecting Japanese interests in Shinju’s challenging environment, the Shindenbutai offer players a distinctive option for their armies.

Yu Jing Action Pack and PanOceania Support Pack

The Yu Jing Action Pack provides players with additional units to enhance their armies, reflecting the faction’s combination of cultural depth and technological advancement. Meanwhile, the PanOceania Support Pack introduces specialized units such as the Trauma-Docs and Machinists, which focus on medical support and technical maintenance to keep PanOceanian forces operational.

JSA Support Pack: The Auxiliary Regiment

The Japanese Secessionist Army (JSA) gains new support options with the Tokusetsu Butai, or Auxiliary Regiment. This unit provides essential medical and technical services, ensuring that the JSA’s front-line forces remain effective. The pack highlights the JSA’s emphasis on a balanced approach to warfare, where support units play a critical role.

Nomads Action Pack: A Faction of Free Spirits

The Nomads, known for their independent and unconventional nature, join the battlefield with their own Action Pack. Originating from three massive spaceships that travel the Human Sphere, the Nomads challenge established norms and offer a unique playstyle. Their focus on creativity and adaptability makes them an appealing choice for players seeking a different approach to the game.

title: The Throne of Thorns II for Ruins of Symbaroum 5E Announced: A Darker, More Epic Chapter Awaits
content:
Free League Publishing has announced The Throne of Thorns II, the latest addition to the Ruins of Symbaroum 5th Edition-compatible game line. This new installment continues the epic six-part campaign set in the world of Symbaroum, with pre-orders now available on Free League’s webshop. Those who pre-order will gain access to an alpha-PDF shortly after purchase via DriveThruRPG.

Scheduled for release in June 2025, The Throne of Thorns II is a 230+ page hardcover book that adapts the third and fourth episodes of the Throne of Thorns chronicle for the 5E ruleset. The campaign is designed for characters of 10th to 14th level and is set against a backdrop of escalating tension and danger. The capital city of Yndaros is in chaos as preparations for a royal wedding unfold, while deadly conspiracies threaten to plunge the Davokar region into war. At the same time, a critical wilderness expedition promises to reshape Ambrian history.

The book includes two full-length adventures, The Darkest Star and Mother of Darkness, which form the mid-section and turning point of the Throne of Thorns campaign. It features nearly 20 color maps detailing various locations, such as towns, forests, and ruins, as well as over 60 stat blocks for non-player characters, including monsters, allies, adversaries, and notable individuals. Additionally, the book provides a collection of handouts to enhance gameplay, offering important information for social challenges and problem-solving.

The Throne of Thorns II requires access to the Ruins of Symbaroum Core Setting books—Player’s Guide, Game Master’s Guide, and Bestiary—to fully utilize its content. Fans of the series can now pre-order the book and gain early access to the alpha-PDF, allowing them to prepare for the adventures ahead of the official release.

title: Vesta Mandate: A Competitive Political Thriller TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
Storygames Chicago has launched Vesta Mandate, a hard sci-fi political intrigue tabletop roleplaying game, on Kickstarter. The campaign will conclude on March 22, offering backers the opportunity to secure the game in either digital or premium hardcover formats.

Set on Vesta Station, a critical hub between Earth and the Outer Rim of the solar system, Vesta Mandate immerses players in a tense political landscape. A century ago, revolutionaries overthrew the Corporation’s control of the station, but now the Vesta Accords are expiring, and the Corporation is returning with threats of force. As members of the Station’s interim government, players take on the roles of ambitious politicians, each with their own vision for the future. Through scheming, negotiation, and betrayal, they must navigate a web of alliances, secrets, and crises to shape the fate of the colony.

Vesta Mandate is a Powered by the Apocalypse (PbtA) storygame enhanced with mechanics and procedures that introduce competitive elements, transforming it into a political drama. Drawing inspiration from games like Pasión de las Pasiones, Carved from Brindlewood, Blades in the Dark, and The Last Caravan, as well as media such as The Expanse, Andor, Silo, and A Memory Called Empire, the game delivers a compelling mix of hard sci-fi and political intrigue.

Designed for 3-5 players, Vesta Mandate can be played as a one-shot or a long-term campaign. Players assume the roles of cunning politicians, each with a Hidden Agenda—a secret plan that evolves into a large-scale coup or power grab. Balancing cooperation and betrayal, players must navigate Secrets, Bonds, and Schisms while responding to escalating crises that threaten the station’s survival.

The game introduces several innovative mechanics to enhance its political drama. Hidden Agendas allow players to co-create secret schemes with the GM, which grow into game-changing power plays. Each character has a scandalous past, known as Secrets, created by other players, which can be used as blackmail. Relationships are central to the game, with Bonds representing alliances and Schisms reflecting conflicts that can escalate into full-blown disputes.

The game uses PbtA-style Moves to resolve tense moments. Players roll two six-sided dice (2d6) and add bonuses based on narrative questions, a mechanic inspired by Pasión de las Pasiones. High-stakes Machinations allow players to burn Bonds for dramatic, game-altering effects.

The game includes five ready-to-run modules, known as Crises, such as Neural Poisoning, Corporate Espionage, and Water Riots. These modules are designed for minimal GM preparation and can be played individually or as part of a larger campaign. Additional Crises are planned as stretch goals.

Backers can choose from a variety of reward tiers, starting at $7 for a digital PDF of the game. Higher tiers include a premium hardcover zine, illustrated by Tony Tran, and a discounted bundle with City of Blood and Plaster, Storygames Chicago’s previous ZineQuest project set in Gilded Age Chicago.

title: Factions Core Rulebook Now Available for Pre-Order
content:
Modiphius Entertainment has announced the pre-order availability of the Fallout: Factions Core Ruleboo. This new hardback rulebook aims to enhance the Fallout: Factions miniature skirmish game, offering players the tools to create campaigns set anywhere in the post-apocalyptic Wasteland.

The Core Rulebook builds on the foundation laid by the Battle for Nuka-World starter set, which featured three raider gangs from Fallout 4’s popular DLC. The new book expands the game’s scope by introducing four additional factions: the Brotherhood of Steel, super mutants, survivors, and raiders. The 112-page, full-color hardcover provides comprehensive rules, campaign systems, and faction-specific content to deepen the gameplay experience.

Priced at £30 / $37, the Core Rulebook will be available for purchase through the Modiphius webstore and local gaming stores in early summer 2025. It is designed to work alongside the Battle for Nuka-World starter set or the upcoming Tokens and Terrain Pack 1, offering players a complete toolkit for creating their own stories in the Wasteland.

The Core Rulebook includes an introduction to wargaming, core rules for fast-paced skirmish gameplay, and an in-depth scenario system to keep each game unique. The Story Phase section allows players to develop their crew, achieve legendary status, or face the consequences of failure. Faction lists provide detailed profiles for each group, including weapons, perks, and legendary characters.

One of the key features of the new rulebook is its flexibility. While the Battle for Nuka-World starter set focused on a specific area, the Core Rulebook allows players to set their campaigns anywhere in the Wasteland. New mechanics, such as Hazards and Facilities, enable crews to customize their Home Turfs, while Objectives and Hazards replace specific scenarios, creating countless combinations for varied gameplay.

Players can also hire new Legends of the Wasteland, upgrade weapons, purchase chems, and unlock perks for their crew. The updated Story Phase ensures campaigns are more expansive and interconnected, offering greater opportunities for storytelling and strategic decision-making.

title: Wrath of the Wyvern: A Dark Fantasy Solo TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
A new dark fantasy solo tabletop role-playing game, Wrath of the Wyvern, has launched on Kickstarter. Set in the Umbral Highlands, a land where humanity struggles to survive under the threat of monstrous wyverns, the game casts players as a lone hunter tasked with reclaiming the world from these fearsome creatures. Inspired by Scottish Celtic mythology, the game blends exploration, survival, and tactical combat into a solo RPG experience.

Wrath of the Wyvern introduces a Fate Card system, which replaces traditional dice rolls. This system, powered by the Fury Engine, is designed to create fast-paced, strategic, and cinematic encounters. Players navigate an open-world hexcrawl, making decisions that influence the fate of the Highlands. The game emphasizes replayability, with branching storylines and faction dynamics adding depth to each playthrough.

Combat is a central element, utilizing a custom Tarot-sized card deck to manage attacks, defenses, and special abilities. Players spend Stamina Points (SP) to execute actions and must adapt to the unique behaviors of their enemies. Survival mechanics, such as hunger, exhaustion, and changing weather conditions, further enhance the exploration experience.

The Umbral Highlands are a perilous and richly detailed world. Players will encounter legendary monsters from Scottish folklore, including the Wulver, Ghillie Dhu, and Kelpie, as well as the game’s primary antagonists: the Sons of Rivesk, ancient and formidable wyverns. Each wyvern battle is a multi-phase event, requiring careful planning and strategy.

In addition to hunting wyverns, players can rebuild Crag Keep, the ruined fortress of the Skyfire Order, and recruit allies to aid in their quest. The game also features arcane powers and legendary weapons, offering players opportunities to wield powerful magic and craft unique tools.

Backers of Wrath of the Wyvern will receive a premium package that includes a 140+ page hardcover rulebook, a massive hexcrawl map of the Umbral Highlands, a Wyvern Showdown battlemap, a hero miniature, and access to the Isle of Skye expansion. The game will be available in English, Spanish, Italian, and French, with each translation handled by a native speaker.

The campaign will run until April 3, giving potential backers 28 days to pledge their support.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.
